- A BOY'S KIM Sitting by a princely child, Never yet by sin defiled, Gazing in his fearless eyes, Who shall picture my surprise'? When I stroked his bonnie hair, And his forehead smooth and fair, Drawing to his lips my hand, Like a knight of Holy Land. As the touch of roses pressed To a sleeping baby's breast,' On my soul I felt a kiss. Match me lady's boon like this! Never ring shall take the place Of this tender kiss of grace; Other lips may never dare Find the secret nestled there. Darling boy, the twilight dies Softer for thy loving eyes; Not a path thy feet have trod But shall wear a greener sod; And thy laughter, glad end low. Lingers where sweet roses grow All the world has something yet Of the kiss I ne'er forget. LFirkoemththeesudbutslte oflriflui eme s d :Led , Some dear hand in mute caress Gave to love and—silentness. Ms. HELEN Mem,
.....*••••••••••1 TIIE JEWS' CEMETERY. (DIDO OF VENICE.)

A tract of sand swept by the salt sea-foam, Fringed with acacia flowers and billowy deep In meadow grasses where tall poppies sleep, And bees athirst for wilding honey roam. Ilow many a bleeding heart hath found its home Under these hillocks which the sea-mews sweep! Here knelt an outcast race to curse and weep, Age after age, 'neath Heaven's unanswering dome! Sai is the place, and solemn, grave by grave, Lost in the dunes, with rank weeds overgrown, Pines in abandonment; as though unknown, 'Encored for, lay the dead, whose records pave This path neglected; each forgotten stone Wept by no moun; :r but the moaning wave.

‘Vnile thus I mused, the genius of the spot Rose in my soul, rebuking me, and said, You wrong these patient and heroic dead. Whose trust, although He slew them, wavered not ! You wrong the living ! Israel ne'er forgot ills forefathers, lapped in earth's narrow bed Each grave is known and namd and numbered. You misconceive the tranquil tragic lot Of lives so fallen on sleep; Secure of God. ISerged in the deathless memory of their race, These wait. And if your callous feet have trod Blank tombs that to the bare skies torn their face. From faith here prostrate learn to kiss the rod, From contrite hope here learn to sue for gram. 3. A. S.

A man of polish who is not welcomed in good society— the bootblack. " Leading Seeley." orchestra.—Punch. A man in Staffordshire once said, speaking of a youth who had married imnrndently, " Why, he didn't want a wife any more'n a tad want's a side-pocket." The witty man of the Middle Temple students said at a City chop honse," I won't pay for steaks as tough as these; PO law Can compel me; they're not legal tender." Little Boy " Papa, are sailors small men ?" Papa : No, my child; why do you ask that ? " Little Boy: "Because I saw the other day that one slept on his watch." It was their first night aboard the steamer. "At last," be said tenderly, "we are all alone, out upon the deep waters of the dark blue sea; and your heart will always beat for ins, as it has beat in the past? " "My heart's all right," she answered, languidly, " but my stomach feels awful." "Are you fond of novels, Mr. Jones ?" "Very !" re- sponded the interrogated gentleman who wished to be thought by the lady questioner fond of literature. "Have you" cmtinned the inquisitive lady, "ever read Ten Thou. sand a Year ?' " " No, madame; I never read that many novels in all my life !" An undergraduate, under examination at Dublin, was missing question after question. At last the examiner got irritated, and said," I declare I've got a dog at home that could answer the questions that have been given to you." "Have you really, sir ?" said the undergraduate, blandly. I "May I ask if you would sell him." They had been engaged to be married 15 years, and still he had not mustered op resolution enough to ask her to name the happy day. One evening he called in a partieular frame of mind, and asked her to sing something tender and touching, something that would "move" him. She sat down at the piano and sang, " Darling, I am growing old." We like the" new pill," which a distinguished physician leas ;lust invented. This invaluable remedy for melancholy is m ehe of "fun ard fresh air, in equal proportions, and is to be taken with cold water three times a day." Having used this article for the last five years, we can vouch for its great virtues. itio says the Woonsocket Patriot. D. Gunther says there are seven thousand species of fish now known to men of science. When a man sits on the ve r hank half a day, watching a cork idly floating on the strain:a, and comes home with a sun-burned nose and not a single specimen of these seven thousand species, he is in. dined to think that Dr. Gunther is a patent medicine adver-

tiser. TEE DELt.TON or "TEA."—Tea, as a meal, is in many latrines a deic-'ea. Although the refreshing cup, accom- panied by a slice or two of bread and butter or toast, may answer the purpose well enough for adults who have the prospect of a supper before going to bed, neither quality nor quanttty is sufficient for young people. Dr. Grosvenor Wilson feelingly remarks, "I have secured to many a child a reas,mable evening meal by suggesting to the mother the mere use of the word 'supper as the name of the third meal." And this is precisely the change that we would wish to see *Atli-dished in every household. It is deplorable to think of he nuinber of hours craving little stomachs suffer without food between the time of going to bed, say at seven o'clock, and rising twelve hours afterwards, not partaking of nour- ishment in the interval, under the impression that suppers are unwholesome. A proper meal in the place of the, oeAi, nary' "tea" will be found to consist in some of the following additions: —Cocoa, made with as much milk as the Paitents can afford; bread and butter, with or without cheese; Istewed fruit hot in the winter, and cold in the summer; a milky rice pudding to which finely-shred beef suet has been added; plain boiled rice and treacle; or, if peiseible; some eggs; cold boiled bacon or meat. The additional ex- pence any of the above articles may appear to entail will not be all loss. Less need will be felt for tonics, from the febrile maladies too often occasioned in early life by children being under-fed. Another demand may also cease, namely for cakes and sweetmeats " to put under the pillow."—Cas- sell's Household .Guide THE HEROINE OF MATAGORDA.—The tempest lasted for I thirty hours, and sixty-four men out of one hundred and forty' had fallen. The fort was not more than one hundred yards square; anti "here," says Napier," be recorded an action of which it is difficult to say whether it were most feminine or heroic." Tbe action referred to, as detailed in " The Eventful Life of a Soldier," won the woman for long after in Scotland the soubriquet of "The Heroine of Mate. erdt." She was the wife of Sergeant Reston, of the Scots Brig ale. Under fire, she tore up her linen to form ban- dages for the wounded ; and water being wanted, a drum- mer boy was ordered to draw some from a well, but the scared child did not seem mach inclined to the task, and lingered at the door of a hut with the bucket in his hand. "Why don't you go for the water ?" asked the surgeon, an- grily. "The pnir bairn is frightened," said Mrs. Reston, and no wonder; gie the bucket to me." And under all thit dreadful storm she proceeded coolly to the well, pro- curing water for the wounded. General Napier states that a shot cat the bucket rope in her hand, but she recovered it, and fulfilled her mission. Her attention to the wounded was beyond all praise, says Sergeant Donaldson, of the 94th; she carried sand bags for the repair of the batteries, and handed ammunition, wine, and water to the men at the , guns. "I think I see her yet," he adds, "while the shot and shell were flying thick around her, bending her body to shield her child from danger by the exposure of her own person." • She died at an old age, in Glasgow, without other token to her merit than that accorded by the humble book of her husband's comrade.—British Battles OIL Land and Sea. GREAT WRITERS AT Worm—Byron sat down to write without any premeditation; his ideas flowed with his ink, and one line suggested the next. But after the poem was Completed, and during its passage through the press, he was continually altering, interlining, and adding. The first copy of "The Giaour" consisted of only 400 lines; to each new edition were added new passages, until it swelled to nearly 1.400 lines Daring the printing of "The Bride of Abydos" he added 200 lines, and many of the original were altered again and again. One of the most constantly labo- rious writers of whom we have any account was Southey. In one of his letters he says: "Imagine me in thie great slaidy of mine (at Geste Hall, Keswick) from bream:lst till dinner, from dinner till tea, and from tea till iitipPC77 in my old black coat, my corduroys alternated with I the -long woritiriiiintaloons and gaiters in one, and thel green shade, anoLsitt,lng at rrty 4esk, 'and na you have y plc- tire and my likaciry4.4- . My 'actions are as regular 25 tlahlef of Saint Diarteatan'i:quarter bags. Three pages of hist after breakfast ; dim to transcribe and copy for press, or to ,make My selections and biographies, or what else salts my hernotir till dinner ti-ne; from dinner till tea I read, writer letters, see the newspaper, and very often in- duir in n....sitstic., After teal go to poetry, and correct and re-write and eopy till lam tired, and then turn to anything, yin-mapper ; and this is my life; which, if it be not a merry I one, is yet as happy as heart could wish." In striking con- trait to this wholly sedentary life was that of his neighbour old fellow poet, Wordsworth. His poems were composed • during his long morning walks upon the mountains, cur- rourded by the scenery, the objects, and the incidents they describe, which thus visually inspired and wrought out his tonceptious. Upon returning home be would go to bed, and while eating his breakfast dictate to an amanuensis.—

A SCIENTIFIC COMMENDATION OF SUN-FLOWEBS.— People who are unfortunate enough to live in damp houses, particularly near andrained land, are apt to think there is no help for them save in removal. They are mistaken. Successful experiments have shown that it is quite possible to materially improve the atmosphere in such neighbour- hoods in a very simple manner—by the planting of the laurel and the sun-flower. The latter gives off an abund- ance of ozone, while the "soulful-eyed" sun-flower is po- tent in destroying the malarial condition. These two, if planted on the most restricted scale in a garden, close to the house, will be found to speedily increase the dryness and salubrity of the atmosphere, and rheumatism, if it does not entirely become a memory of the past, will be largely alle- viated. Few people are aware of the anti-malarial proper- ties of the " ultra-poetical, super-msthetical" sun-flower.—

Kingdom, big or little, a landowner, and holder in the Unite*: instead of being the 91,,min0al owner, he shall be the absolute a cation of titles some- e simpli owner of the "fee simple, . iv..et But pending such a who'll, thing might be done. An of Parliament might be for the titles to landed passed creating District Regi.4triea' property, like we have now Distrk Registries for the : proving of Wills ;or there might !Ar other department erica. It was added to the existing County Courts, al!, iu stated in evidence before the Select Ccananitt on Land Titles and Transfer that "there are between gh"l.o ant: 1,000 deeds dealing with land executed in England every day' which makes 300,000 in one year." Of these it le estimated that more than one-fourth are freehold transferee Why should not the new. Act of Parliament make it compuloory that the titles to all land changing hands after a certain date should be registered immediately, without any option to the lawyer concerned? It might be further enacted that on and after a certain date no document purporting to deal with land should be valid until it was registered. Many working details and difficulties would present themselves for solution, but they would be overcome here as they have been in other countries, and the ultimate object ever kept steadily in view should be that finally every plot of land in this country should appear on the register as the property of some person or persons having absolute power to deal with that property and confer a complete title on a purchaser, subject only to charges appearing on the face of the register. The very fact that the title was so registered would at once I enhance the future value of that land, and this alone would lead many owners who were not selling to register their titles voluntarily. This would be a great step in the right direc- tion, and in time, as all land was gradually made "free," and changed hands, every plot of land in the whole country would appear on the registers. By proceeding thus by degrees' anything like a great block of business will be avoided, though the legal profession will have ample occu- pation for years to come, and even after the registration of all titles there will be such an increased traffic in land that the regulation fees on the numerous sales will probably equal the present remuneration of the lawyers. Such is a brief sketch of the Reform necessary to make "Free Land," described by Mr. Fowler, M.P. (Cambridge), as" a reform which would leave all natural forces to work out their proper results with perfect freedom, so that our vast wealth as a nation, may be used in the development of our soil, unburdened by laws which are unworthy of a free and intelligent people ;" while an eminent foreign writer, M. de Laveleye, writes, "It is of the highest public inieret!, in the first place, that landed property should easily get into those hands by which it can be turned to the best account; secondly, that the title to property in land should be secure and incontestable; and, thirdly, that there should be no legal obstacles to the sub-division of land when the natural economy tends to it, so that the number of small landowners should not be artificially reduced by imperfec- tion in the law. As long as England does not introduce security, publicity, facility of exchange, in fact, free trade into everything connected with property in land, there will ever be an insuperable obstacle to the establishment of an agrarian system in keeping with the wants of modern society. A reform in this particular branch of English law is, in my opinion, the most urgent of all." Such a reform would gradually, naturally, and legiti- mately tend to spread the ownership of the land of this country among much greater numbers, and we cannot do better than conclude with the statesmanlike words of the Marquis of Ripon (himself a great landholder), at Bristol, not long ago :—" The laws of every country must favour either the distribution or the centralisation of property, and I have no hesitation in saying, for my own part, that the time has now fully arrived when the law of England ought to favour as much as possible a free and unfettered use of the land by the actual present owner, and that it ought to promote the distribution and not the centralisation of landed property." If the voters of this country realised the importance of " Free Land" it would be made a test question for every Parliamentary Candidate, to whichever Party he professed to belong.

A CURE FOR STOPPED TIP Sl:MS.—Care mast be taken that the main drain does not become closed up by the de- posit of fat that comes from washing up ntens;l3 that have held fatty substances. This is very important, and it is astonishing how little aware good housekeepers, to say no- thing of ordinary domestic servants, are of its import. In the old system of drainage, when everything went direct into a cesspool or large sewer, there was no risk of obstruc- tion from fat, and the fact of such an obstruction was un- known. In the new system with the small drain the risk lof obstruction is great. The servant who pours the greasy water as a fluid down the sink, does not for a moment think that after a short time the fat will separate from the water, and in the cold drain deposit In the solid form. Yet that is what happens, and in the space of two or three, months it frequently occurs that the drain is effectively blocked from se simple a cause. The plan to adopt in order to prevent this accident is to see that, once every month at least, the drain pipe is well and completely cleared of fat by means of hot water charged with soda. One pound of common wash- ing soda dissolved in two gallous of boiling water forms the most effective clearing solution. Some of this solution poured down the sinks clears them in their passages to the main drain, and a few gallons poured through the man-hole at the top of the drain down the main drain clears that so as to allow the brushto pass readily through.—Good Words How THE OCEAN as Kinn ,Cutan.—COmmon salt bas a considerable affinity for watee, in 'which it freely dissolves, one hundred parts of watet dissolving about thirty-five parts of salt.- Curiously enough, cold water dissolves almost as umeh as wars water. This is an exception to the general rule. The attraction between water and salt produces some results which are sufficiently remarkable. The following. simple _experiment will illustrate this. Take two glass jars, or two plain glass tumblers will do, and 611 them withl water; dissolve in one of them a few grains of common-. salt, and add to both somesommon white china-clay, stil-1 riiig them well up, so that the lay is well diffused through' the water, rendering it opaque. Care must betaken not to stir the one without the salt with the rod used to stir the one with salt. After stirring put both aside, and note how long the clay takes to settle in each jar, and the water be- comes clear and transparent. A most remarkable difference will he noticed between the two. The water containing the salt in solution will be quite clear in about one or two hours, according to the quantity of salt dissolved, while the pure water will not be clear for twenty-four, or even thirty-six hours, if the water we use is very pure ana soft. We see from this that the attraction of the salt for the water pre- vents the latter from holding the particles of clay in sus- pension. The rosette flowing from this action of salt on water are very striking and important. The waters of the ocean, as we all know( hold in solution a considerable quan- tity of salt; about three parts in a hundred is the average; in,fact, it is like our tumbler or jar of water, to which we have added a few grains of salt, and consequently cannot, retain in suspension for any length of time finely-divided mitter—such as clay or sand. The obvious action of the salt, therefore is to keep the ocean clear; all mad or silt is rapidly precipitated to the bottom and forms those vast deposits found all over the bottom Of the ocean in the dredg- ing operations of the Challenger. stud other vessels. Further we know that the rivers of the world carry down to the sea immense quantities of worn-down, rocks and soil. During flood we see our own comparatively puny rivers rendered quite brown and muddy from the amount of suspended matter which they carry along with them on their courses. Some of the more gigantic rivers of other countries are never clear, but are laden during the whole year with large I,quantities of this rock and soil waste, grinding down in thei course of time the mountains and hills of the dry land, and catryina them into the midst of the sea. The waters of the Mississippi, for instance, are always muddy, and if we fill a jar from this river, it will remain muddy and opaque for days. Now let us considerwhat happens when the mud- laden water reaches the sea. If we happen to live near the ooast, 14 us get a little:sea-water and Mix it with fresh water, in which we have stirred up a little clayoand note the result. The clay will be rapidly precipitated, and the water rendered clear. Now this is exactly what happens at the mmtbs of rivers—the mud and silt are at once pre- cipitated where the river and sea-waters meet. This is the reason why it is so difficult to keep the mouths of rivers and harbours clear of silt. We are compelled to use our dredg- ing-machines continually, or they would rapidly be danger - oats to navigation.—Science for All. 'THE COMING Worms.—One of my August Notes wat on "The Abnormal Weather of 1881." I there endeavoured to show that the excessive cold which we suffered in Eng- land last winter was a result of increased solar activity, and consequent higher mean temperature of the earth's sur- face and atmosphere, and explained this apparent paradox as due to an exaggeration of the usual interchange of the tropical and Arctic atmospheric currents. The great move, ments of oar atmosphere (sstting aside the minor disturb- ances) consist in an upper flow of heated air from the tropics towards the poles, and a lower flow of cold air from the polar towards the tropical regions. The trade-winds are a portion of the latter. We are in the region of the "vari- ables," ie. where the tropical winds have been sufficiently cooled to sometimes graze the earth and thus contend with the Arctic flow. Such being the case, an excessive general beating of the air may carry more hot air northward over our heads and cause a greater quantity of sold northern air to flow upon the surface at our latitudes; for it must be re- membered that these atmospheric currents are due to the differences of temperature, not to absolute heat, and that the supposed greater sun-heat would have but little effect on the temperature of the ice-covered portions of the Arctic regions, TbeinelsoDlargelys wife* inuelelnev ttiedWerk of t.hawiegf. Recent intelligence confleios my speculations Theachalings vestiels being intelligencee'of AttaOrdilrY inovement.of the pack-ice in the Arctic seas, which was taking place at' about the time I was writing. It is reported to have de- scended 500 miles farther south than usual in that open stretch of Arctic sea north of Europe and east of Greenland. fn consequence of this, Spitztorgen and Novaya Zemlya have been unapproachable this year. and the Dutch Arctic expedition has turned back, finding farther progress impos- sible. On the other hand, Lieut. Greely, on his arrival at Franklin Bay, west of Greenland, found open water exten- ding. as far as the eye could reach How will this affect us during the forthcoming winter? This is a pretty meteoro- logical problem, which I find easier to propound than to solve. It may be that a great extension of the usual ice- boundary directly to the north of our islands may cool down a large body of air that will reach and sweep over us and bring with it a very bitter winter; or, on the other hand, the unusually great quantity of cold water that will flow as an undercurrent southwards, in consequence of thecooling due to the thawing of so much ice by the salt water' may Push a large volume of the Gulf Stream northward, and thus increase the warmth it usually brings to our coasts. In the present limited state of our meteorological knowledge, it is difficult te say which may prevail. It is most probable that the battle between the two influences will be fought hereabouts, and we shall witness the conflict in the form of violent storms and sudden changes; abnormally warm winter weather when the south-west winds prevail, with intervals of severe cold when the north and east are victorious, with dense sea-fogs wherever they are intermixed. The consola- tion which such a prospect offers is that the final result of an additional supply of sup-heat, such as the American continent has lately felt, and an excessive southward drift of Arctic ice, must ultimately bring us more warmth and better harvests. If our chief climatic enemy, the accumu- lation of Arctic ice, is considerably diminished, we may ex- pect a cycle of hot summers and mild winters, and harvests to correspond; but I doubt whether anybody can safely pre- dict when this will commence. It may be as near to us as Piazzi Smyth has supposed, or it may be delayed a year or two longer.— The Gentleman's Magazine.

A dairy house has recently been built on the Experi- mental Farm of the Illinois Industrial University, which it is designed to make a "Dairy Experimental Station" so far as may be found practicable. Professor Morrow announces his readiness to receive and test any new apparatus or pro- case which may be submitted to him, and to report on its merits. . The shipments of merino sheep to Texas, Colorado, and other Western States and territories is large and rapidly in- creasing. There seems to be a growing tendency to im- prove the grade of wool in these sections, and fine wool sheep are correspondingly encouraged. Prices rule high for first-class merino rams, several sales having been re- cently made by Eastern parties at 1,500 dots. to 2,000 dots. each. JIBBING HORSES.—' have long waited an opportunity to disclose a mode by which a jibbing horse can be made to proceed without cruelty or danger. Jibbing is the result of a temporary mental state, and the object in view ehould be to divert the small mind of the horse from its one prevail- ing idea. I had a fine mare that once now and then would jib, but we felt no annoyance and endured but little delay. I would tell the coachman to do nothing, above all not to whip her. I would alight and jingle my keys near her ear. This was the first step to divert her mind. I would then pat her and pass my hand down the leg and lift up her fore foot ; then, with a piece of stone, my pocket knife, or a large coin, hammer on her shoe a few times, and on drop- ping her foot we were ready for a fresh start without further trouble. If I were not present, the groom could do it. Allow me to remark that this process may not be the best to divert the thought of a horse, but the principle to be borne in mind is to change the prevailing idea. To this end two other modes, among many, may be adopted :-1. For the driver of a jibbing horse to be provided with a small bottle of something that a horse abhors, and which stings or irri- tates ; by placing a small portion on the tongue of the horse, all its thought is directed to clear its month, and every other consideration is clean gone from its mind. 2. A small portion of something that is offensive to the sense of smell of a horse may be placed near or on its nostril. He will snort, sneeze, and think no more of his jib.—A Country F.S.A., in" The Times." Limn RENTS No GAIN.—My friend dates his experience of farming back over half a century. Fifty years ago, said he, we had no " artificial " bills, but we grew several more bushels per acre of grain than now. Cultivation was neater in every respect, more pride being taken by the men in all the processes of the farm. Further, many of the ills that both live stock, the land, and the crops now suffer from were unknown. He knew nothing of science ; some of its discoveries might be beneficial, but from what he had seen of general results he believed, comparing the past with the present, that we were fast poisoning the land, the crops,and our live stocks to boot. Said he, "You will never make me believe that sound, good crops can be grown with vitriol and such like ' pussen !' (poison)." By this time we had arrived at the destination of our walk—a small property of 13 acres of grass land in Furness. Here, said he, is a bit of land that affords an illustration of the manner in which much of the land of the kingdom has been treated of late years. Twenty years ago this land was left by my brother- in-law in trust for my sister and her children. The trustees were tradesmen. The land was in splendid "heart." It was let by ticket to the highest bidder, carter, jobber, butcher, or anyone who would give the highest rent. I cautioned the trustees what the final result would be— namely, that the land would be ultimately dear to the tenant without the payment of a rent. At one letting, the 13 acres brought £72 ; but scarce a year passed without, some of the tenants of the fine fields failing to pay the rents. Year by year the rents have declined, until now they fail to get an offer at any price. This, said he, is just the course too many landlords have pursued of late years, impelled thereto either by greed or necessity. The trustees were not over courteous, told me that farmers were always grumbling about rents, that the land was there, the tenants could not run away with it, and that they intended to make the most of it—that is, to get the highest possible rents. They have lost more in unpaid rents than they would have received if let at a reasonable rent, and now we shall see the state the land is in. I have never been over it from that day to this. We walked over the land, and anything more disheartening could scarcely be. It was, as my friend had predicted." dear at any price," and, worse still, the writer is the trustee of the original trustee, and has the duty of providing the widow with the means of existence from such a wornemat legacy. He asks the same question as many other landlords of the present day, "How is it to be done ?" —" R," in Agricultural Gazette. The average prices were—wheat 425. 2d. per quarter, barley 345. 7d., and oats 21s. 6d.--Preston: Wheat 636 quarters, barley nil, and oats 11. The average prices were—wheat 395. 7d. per quarter, barley nil, and oats 265. 10d. —Manchester : Wheat 6,305 quarters, barley 123, and oats 1,537. The average prices were—wheat 41s. 7d., barley 241. 9d., and oats 20s. 9d.— Ulverston : Wheat 149 quarters, barley nil, and oats 95. The average prices were—wheat 445. 5d., . barley nil, and oats 253. —.Lancaster : Wheat 194 quar- ters, barley nil, tuft oats nil. The average prices were— wheat 435. 10d. per quarter, barley nil, and oats nil.— , TViyan : Wheat 101 quarters, barley nil, and oats 1,544. 1 The average prices were—wheat 375. 61 per quarter. barley nil, and oats 20s. 2d. / On Wednesday, a singular scene was witnessed at Yedingham, near Halton, where there was a gathering of farmers and others in a field in front of the Vicarage, to hear an address from Mr. John Elsworth, farmer, of Yeding- ham, who by circular had announced his intention of "reading a paper and giving a short address on the vicar of Yedingham and his late tenant." Mr. Elsworth's address was on agricultural questions generally, but more especially with reference to the relations between himself, as tenant of the glebe farm, and the vicar of the parish, the Rev. F. Porter. In the course of a long and interesting speech, Mr. Elsworth spoke of the necessity for an improvement in the land laws of this country. He had taken the glebe farm in 1841 of the Rev. John Ellis, a former vicar, and afterwards obtained a lease enabling him to keep it in his own hands till five years ago, when he put his two sons upon it. He had erected new farm buildings, house, and stables, and done a great deal to the place altogether, for none of which he had go't any return, and his sons were now compelled to leave the place. In the valuation he was actually made to pay for the alteration of buildings to which the vicar had never contributed anything, and also for over-cropping some land, which was sown by the succeeding tenant directly after. These and other questions, together with a lot of personal matters between himself and the vicar and his carates, were listened to by the audience with a great amount of interest. Mr. Elsworth especially condemned, in strong terms, -the Agricultural Holdings Act. The death is announced of Lord Curriehill, Lord of Session in Scotland, at the age of 54 years. He was called to the Bar in 1851, and was promoted to the Bench in 1874. At the York Assizes on Tuesday three men, who were arrested in this city on a charge of forging the notes of two Yorkshire banks, were sentenced to penal servitude—one for 14, another for 10, and the other for seven years. BRUTAL MURDER BY A FATHER.—On Saturday morning Sergeant-Major Redding, at Doncaster, took one of his chil- dren into the cellar and beat it to death with a stone. Red- ding, who is believed to be sane, is in custody. On Monday the magistrates at Queenstown sent eight seamen of the Liverpool Ship Pampero to gaol for six weeks for insubordination and refusing to work. The master, who was c onvitced of assariting two of his crew, was fined £5. The inquiries at Oldham into the American cotton frauds are bringing some strange facts to light. It is stated that one bale has been found to contain 6pb. of old iron, and another some loamy substance weighing more than the cotton itself I Last year the tea duty, at Gl. per lb., amounted to £3,870,655, the quantity being 154,824,0201b5. taxed. Some idea of the consumption of dried fruit may be gathered from the fact that the duty on currants, figs, raisins, &c., reached £492,751 last year. At a meeting on Thursday of the committee of the Bir- mingham Liberal Club, presided over by Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., it was decided to erect new club premises in the vicinity of the Town Hall for the accomodation of a thousand members, at a cost, including the site, of about £60,000. Lord O'Ha,an, the late Lord Chancellor of Ireland, has been invested with the dignity of a Knight of St. Patrick. His Lordship is the third Roman Catholic on the roll of Knights of St. Patrick, the two others being the Earls of Kenmare and Granard. The investiture will be held in St Patrick's Hall early in January. In the case of the fatal railway collision at Desford, near Leicester, the coroner's jury on Monday returned a verdict of " manslaughter " against Thomas Butler, the pointsman, and the railway officials were blamed for not having fitted . .

VII.

the express with a continuous brake, and for certain acts oi negligence in connection with the signalling and the facing points. A Dublin paper gives an amusing account of the dispersal of a meeting of the Castlecomer branch of the Ladies' Land League. The leaders of the meeting would argue with the police the question of their authority to interfere with the assembly, and a resolution was passed Protesting against the " unwelcome presence of two policemen," and demanding from them an exrl illation, "as according to one of the rules of the League gentlemen are not allowed." In the Dublin Ga:ette on Tuesday a return of agrarian outrages was published as furnished to the Inspector Gen,eral of the Royal Irish Constabulary during the month ending with October 31. Under the head of intimidation by threat- ening letters and otherwise there are returns of 306 cases, and the total return of " outrages " amounts to 490. Seven outrages are returned under the head of killing, cutting or maiming cattle, and 52 under that of incendiary fires. Four- teen cases of firing into dwellings are reported, and 49 cases of injury to property. The suppression of the Irish Land League has been followed by a resuscitation of the Home Rule League, of which little has been heard during the last two years, and an address from the Association to the Irish people has been issued. It bears no signatures. It speaks of the accursed Union of 1800, and advises agitation " until the infamous usurpation is undone." The address declares that in no country in the world, "except, perhaps, Russia." is there so little public liberty left and so much despotism exercised as in Ireland. A Conference of ministers of religion and others desirous of promoting the principles of peace was held on Tuesday, at Leeds, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Jackson., Several members of Parliament, including Mr. A. Peace, Mr. Richard, and Mr. Illingworth were present. A letter was read from the Bishop of Manchester, who had been invited but was unable to attend, expressing sympathy with the objects of the Conference Resolutions were passed in favour of international arbitration, definingthe duty of the Christian churches towards this question, and expressing regret at the enormous and ever increasing armaments by which Europe is over-run, and which constitute "a scandal to Christianity and civilization." A public meeting was held in the evening. The Timmer of an old farmer is reported from Retford. George Hardy, 71 years of age, lived with his wife and two servants at North %Vheatley. On Sunday night his wife left the house to go to chapel. When she returned her husband was not in the house, and one of the men servants went out to look for him, and found him lying on his back in the yard covered with blood. He had been beaten about, the head in a terrible manner, and by his side lay a fork which was smeared with blood. Mr. Superintendent San- ford and Mr. Inspector -R. J. Sanford, of Retford, arrived soon after midnight, and at half-past four on Monday morn- ing returned to Retford with a young man named Herbert Snell. one of the servants, who is supposed to be the mur- derer. A fork had been thrust eight inches into Hardy's head. Ills pockets had been emptied, and everything he had about him taken away. ELOPEMENT OF A FARMER'S WlFE.—During the past week the quiet village of Longton, near Preston' was thrown into great commotion by the discovery that the wife of a substantial and respected farmer of that neighbourhood had eloped. For some time back a good looking young fellow had been employed as a labourer on thefarm, and an inti- macy sprang up between him and the farmer's wife, a bloom- ing, buxom woman, about 30 years of age. The intimacy was noticed, it seems, by almost everybody but the farmer himself, who, however, was apprised of it by some of his neighbours, and a quarrel with his spouse, and the dismissal of the young labourer, were the consequences. The sins of the wife, however, were condoned, and the couple seemed to have resumed their previous quiet life, when a few days ago the woman disappeared, leaving Longton under the pretext of visiting her relatives in Preston. Her husband was from home at the time, after his return next day awaited her re- appearance until the following day, when it came to his knowledge that the ci decant labourer had left the village simultaneously with his wife. A woman answering her des- cription in every particular has been making inquiries at the office of a shipping agent in Preston, relative to assisted passiges to New 'Zealand, the best farming districts of America, Sze., and " whether she could book to America under anether name." There is now no doubt that the couple have gone away tokether, the woman leaving behind her a daughter ten years of age. BOARD OF TRADE RETtnNs.-The Board of Trade returns for October, issued on Monday, show that the total declared value of the exports for the month was £21,223,081, against £18,685.060 for the same month in 1880, and £17,699,432 in 1879. The total value of the exports for the past ten months is £193,043,703, against £185,731,037 for the same period in 1880, and £157,875,597 in 1879. The total value of the imports in October was £31,307,313, against £27,436,060 in October 1880, and £32,316,565 in October. 1879. The total value of the imports for the 10 months of the year is £328,151,306,again5t £337,843,822 in 1880, and £292,462797 lin 1879. In the ten months the cotton imported amounted to 12,398,724 cwt., as compared with 11,136.663 for 1880, and 9,854,111 for 1879; cotton exported, 1,466,773 cwt., as against 1,615,907, and 1,364,974; cotton yarn, 209,852,900 lbs. as against 175,697,100 and 193,747200 respectively; cotton piece goods, 3.984,206,600 yards, as compared with 3,697,540,800 and 3,070,814,800 yards. The export of cotton yarn during Oct. was 21,138,200 lbs., as against 20,853,500 in Oct. 1880, and 20,860,400 in 1879. Cotton piece goods exported in 1880, and 351,338,700 in 1879. The value of the cotton yarn exported in the month was £1,094,062,158 against £1,086,921 in October, 1880; and of piece goods, £5,122,417 as compared with £4,896,112, in Oct., 1880. AN OUTRAGED HUSBAND.—At the Manchester assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Kay. James Johnson, 44, con- victed of unlawfully wounding William Yarwood, at Barton- upon-Irwell, on the 29th August, was put up for sentence.— His Lordship said the prisoner burst open the door of the house of the prosecutor, who was his next-door neighbour, and found Yarwood in the very act !of adultery with the prisoner's wife. Ile struck Yarwood on the head with a cleaver, a blow which fractured his skull, and for some time his life was in danger. The jury had to consider whether, in doing that act, the prisoner had formed any deliberate intent to injure the man. The jury decided that the prisoner had no felonious intention, but found the prisoner guilty of unlawfully wounding. He had no reason to be dissatisfied with the verdict of the jury. The provocation given to the prisoner was one of the greatest a man could receive. It was— The inexpiable wrong, the unutterable shame, That turns the clward's heart to steel. The sluggard's blood to flame. , The effect of the verdict, his Lordship continued, is this. That you committed the act for which you now stand in that dock under an uncontrollable impulse of passion, ex- cited in you by suddenly seeing this outrage committed upon you. I shall treat you on that assumption. If your criminality be any greater—l have no right to suppose it so—and if you deserve any greater punishment than that I am going to pronounce,l leave you in the hands of God. I will not punish you. I require you te enter into your' own recog- nisances in the sum of £lOO to come up for judgement when \ you shall be called upon.—The result was received in court with applause, which was of course at once, suppressed. I Mr. Gladstone and other members of the Cabinet were present at the Lord Mayor's banquet on Wednesday. The Premier, responding to the toast of Her Majesty's Ministers, delivered a short speech, in which he referred with satisfac- tion to the perceptible improvement in the condition of Ireland. and indicated the necessity for entering upon the task of reforming the procedure of the House of Commons in order to make that House adequate to discharge the business of the country. Earl Granville in responding to the toast of the House of Peers dwelt at some length on his special "hobby," foreign affairs. Speaking of the Turco-Greek settlement, he complimented the Turkish Commissioner on his anxiety throughout to arrive at a satisfactory termination of the difficulty. On Egyptian affairs, the noble Earl said the French were in perfect agreement with this country. The ' negotiations for a treaty with France were then noticed, and it was remarked that the conclusion of a treaty was not so snitch of commercial as of political importance, and however anxious the Government might be to to have a treaty they felt it difficult to go against the wish of Parliament crr the desire of the country. The favourite topic of Sir H. Drum- mond Wolff and other provincial speakers—the Washington Treaty—was alluded to in connection with the affairs of Ireland; and the Foreign Secretary rejoicing in the better feeling between this country and the great Republic, asked if Mr. Forster's onerous task would kayo been relieved if the violent action of the Land League had found a ready sym- pathy on the part of the Americans, exasperated by what they considered an intolerable wrong inflicted on themselves.

Mr. Whittaker, of Edenfield, writes to a contempory in reference to a letter by "J. W." on the above subject, as follows : "I have been taking your paper for nearly forty years, and take great interest in reading anything about farming, as I have been a great sufferer. My father said, over forty years ago, ' Always take care not to spend much money on other people's property." But I have disregarded his ad- vice altogether. I have seven farms, and have spent more money on most of them than I have paid rent, and most of I them are from £3 to £4 per statute acre, and now I am pay- jug for my own improvements. Some of the landlords have raised the rent over 50 per cent. Most of the farms we have had from thirty to forty years, with no leases, except one where I live. This farm was sold in 1863, and I then had twelve years to do of my lease. The new landlord spent about £3OO in five years, and I spent more than double. He then said, without being asked, ' I will lengthen your lease; what length must I make it?' I said,' A hun- dred years, if you like.' So he got one made for 99 years. We now get doable crops from this farm. If all the land in England was properly farmed it would grow more than double the crops, but so long as tenants have no security, how can they expect them to improve their farms? I would not advise anyone to do as I have done. 'Talking about Irish land laws, we want them here as bad as any- where. We have at present 110 horses, three traction en- gines, 30 cows, and 100 sheep, and we grow about 3,000 yards of hay per year, and buy more till every year than we make. I have been trying very hard for many years to get more leases, but cannot get any; so I have given up asking them. If I ask some of them for anything to be done, they tell me that if I don't like I can leave them, as they can get more rent. This is poor encouragement, after having made their farms worth double the rent. I could say ten times more if I had time. The letter in your paper by 'J. W.' is quite correct. You can make what use you think proper of this letter." Soon after the great potato famine in Ireland in 1849-50, many of the Irish landlords, owing to the system of entails described in previous articles, and the almost total cessation of rents in consequence of the deep and protracted distress, were reduced to such a state of embarrassment that what was known as the Encumbered Estates Court was estab- lished by Act of Parliament. Its objects were—first, to ob- tain the means of enforcing the compulsory sale of an en- cumbered estate, and, secondly, to give to the purchaser a parliamentary title. Under that Act, and through the in- strumentality of that ' Court, landed estates worth £20,000,000 were compulsorily sold, involving no fewer than 7,000 conveyances. The result was to pass this enormous quantity of land out of the hands of those embarrassed owners, utterly unable from their straitened circumstances to make the most of it, into the possession of those capable of developing its cultivation. Has not the time arrived when something of the kind is required in England ? If an encumbered life tenant, weighed down with mortgages, annuities, and jointures—as we have already seen many of them are—is unable to meet his liabilities, why should not his creditors have the power to compel a sale of the estate through the medium of some duly constituted court, so that their claims may be met, and the land thereby pass, as a whole or in separate lots, to people who have the ability and the inclination to improve it, and thereby benefit the whole community by increased employment of labonr and production of food? Many English estates are now as much encumbered as Irish Es- tates were immediately after the potato famine; and if some such court were established in this country there is little doubt that many an embarrassed life tenant, with the concurrence of the tenant in tail, would voluntarily sell the property through the court. Only those who have hid experience know the extent to which the title to these encumbered estates are complic- ated and open to question and doubt, and it would not be the leest advantage of such a Court, that it would give to a purchaser a Parliamentary title, which would be absolutely good and free from cavil, and therefore marketable and without the least difficulty. If the English Land Question is to be comprehensively and thoroughly dealt with, the creation of such a Court Get all the fresh air you can. It is beneficial in every wil, be indispensable. Mr. Baron Huddleston and Justice Hawkins DA 'afore 11 them on Monday an application in Lamb POW' ,1!: was an action to recover damages for the breach of a 00111 Y" to marry, and at the trial before Mr. Justice Watkin Hams, at Warwick, the jury found a verdict for the plain. tiff, damages, £l,ooo.—Mr. Mellor, Q.O now, on behalf of the defendant, moved for a rule calling upon the plaintiff to show cause why there should not be a new' trial/ uP01:1 the Founds that the learned Judge should have non-snited the plaintiff ; that the verdict was against the weight scr evidenCe, and that the damages were excesSive. A commercial treaty between France and Austria was bigned on Monday, and the old treaty has been renewed for three months. The German Charg4 d'Affaires at Constantinople has I presented to the Porte a Note concerning the detention of the steamer Vulcan, in which he maintains.that, with regard to vetsels passing through the Dardahellee and the Bosphor- eus, the Turkish Government has no right to examine caigo consignzd to foreign ports. _ A despatch from Astrachan states that the railway ken Tiflis to Baku is nearly completed, A. St. Petersburg tele- gram states that a survey is nearly completed for a military line to Kars, and that it is proposed to construct two other lines to the Persian frontier, which 'when constructed ,add enormously to Use military etrength of Russia in that finPortant;region. THE BRIGHTON RAILWAY MUDM!

The trial of Lefroy for the murder of Mr. Gold on the Brighton Railway was remedied at Maidstone Assizes on Saturday, before Lord Chief ustice Coleridge. Detective- sergeant Holmes gave an account of the retnrn with Lefroy to Wallington. lie regarded. Mm as the injured man, not- withstanding that he received a telegram on the way stating that a body had been found, and there was no watch upon it, and that he had better take the number of Lefroy's watch. Even when Lefrcry gave the wrong number and did not know the name of the maker, his suspicions were not aroused until he 'received a subsequent telegram, after he left the prisoner. He secured the number and the name of the maker, which corresponded with that of MrzGold's watch. Evidence was next given as to Lefroy leeving the house, as hestated, to see Mr. Cressy, a surgeon, which he never did. One of the pawnbroker's assistants spoke posi- tively to him as the man who redeemed a pistol on the morning of the murder, and another had a strong belief that he was the man. Further evidence was given that it would have been impossible for any one to have left the train. 1,1 the course of the day Clayton, with whom the prisoner lodged, declared that he was at honte on the day he was alleged to have pawned some goods, and said lie had kept the statement back for the triaL He 'NM ordered to leave the box by the Judge on Monday. The evidence given related principally to the •prizoner's concealment and arrest at Stepney. Before the defence was opened. the witness named Weston, whose statements as to what took place when Lefroy arrived at Brighton were the subject of much comment, endeavoured 'to obtain a hearing for three witnesses, who, he said, would corroborate his evidence, but the 3udge refused to allow him to proceed. Mr. Montagu Williams then delivered an elaborate speech for the defence. He accounted for Lefroy's trip to Brighton by saying that be went to meet a young lady, and then set up the "third man theory" in support of his client's assertion that he had been assaulted and robbed, He dwelt particularly on the fact that the prisoner,was never known to have had a pistol in his possession, pointed out the doubt there was as to his having pledged or re- deemed one on the day of the murder, and declared that "the third man" could have escaped from the train in Clayton Tunnel or even passed out unnoticed at Preston or Brighton. The Attorney-General, in replying, contended 1 that no one could have left the train unnoticed, and that the whole conduct of the prisoner pointed to him as the mut.* darer. The Judge summed up on Tuesday, from which it would appear that he was absolutely convinced of the pri- soner's guilt. The jury was only engaged for ten minutes in considering their verdict, and they found the prisoner guilty. The Judge passed sentence, and intimated to the convict that there was no hope of mercy. Lefroy turned to the Jury and said that "some day, when it was too late, they would learn that they had murdered him." He was removed to the gaol at Lewes, where the sentence will be carried out.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

- - Bannow-rts-FunsEss, Morinat —The demand for hema- tite pig iron remains very steady, and the market this-morn- ing is reported strong. The consumption of all qualities of pig iron is being considerable; and tile output is exceedingly large throughout the district. Makers. have large orders in hand, and the demand seems likely to maintain the heavy amount of work which is at present passing through their hands. Prices show no variation. No. 1 Bessemer is worth 62s ed per ton, and No. 2 forge 'des at works. Stocks are inconsiderable. Steel rails are in large output, as also are blooms, and the foreign consnmption of both these classes of metal is heavy. Iron ore is in good demand, at rather fuller prices. Coal sells well.. Coke in full delivery. LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAIn—The advance, both in prices and wages, is now general throughout the coal trade of this 'district, and at the West Lancashire collieries, which were stopped last week, work has now been resumed, although some restriction of the output is talked of. There has been ' rather a slackening off during the week in the demand for the better classes of round coal, but the general tone of the trade continues healthy, and colliery proprietors are firm at their advanced rates. The milder weather, couplet with the heavy buying last month in anticipation of the upward movement in values, has naturally tended to curtail the requirements of consumers for house-fire purposes, but colliery proprietors have mostly deliveries to make on account of orders already in hand sufficient to keep their pits fully going for the present, and any falling off in the demand consequently does not yet make itself felt. The lower classes of round coal for iron-making and general trade purposes continue in fairly good demand, though with- out any actual pressnre for supplies. Engine classes of fuel move off moderately well, but with the large quantity of round coal now being screened, slack is still at many col- I lieries going into stock. rrices remain about the same as I those given last week, and although in some cases high% figures are quoted, the average rates at the pit mouth are about 10s, per ton for best house coal, 83. 6d. seconds, 7s. for good qualities of steam and forge I coal, ss. for good burgy, •es. 6d. to 4s. for good siasic, and at these prices sellers generally are firm. There is but little material change to notice in the condition of the iron trade. So far as pig iron is concerned the market continues quiet but Steady; whilst for finished iron a good demand is maintained at full rates; and in the engineering branches of trade there is an increasing quantity of work coming in, both on home and foreign account, especially in toola and machinery of various descriptions. Although the transactions in pig iron have for the last few weeks been very limited, makers prices have not been materially affected except where their quotations had been put up to a figure considerably above the current range of prices; in which cases more disposition has been shown to meet the market on a reasonable basis. Local finished-iron makers contir.ue very busy.. Large purchases for shipment have been made during the week, and home-trade requirements are increas- ing. For delivery into the Manchester district prices are firm, at £6 10s. to £6 15s. for bars, £7 55...£7 10s. for hoops, and £8 105. to £9 15s. for sheets.

On arriving at Noirthwich Mr. Owen drove to the residence of Dr. Wolsey, who pronounced life to be extinct, and the body was then removed to an adjoin- ing hotel to await the post mortem examination and inquest. The doctor also attended to Ford's injuries, and expressed the opinion that they might result fatally. He was taken back in the trap to High Legh, and the three surviving poachers were taxen to the Police Station at Lyrem, where they were handed over to Sergeant Harrington, of the county constabulary. They gave the names of James Perrin, John Hitchen, and Thomas Willis, describing thernselvee as rock- salt getters, alr of Northwich. Hitchen's head was severely damaged, and had to be dressed; the services of a medical man were required in Perrin's case, his skull having come into violent contact with some weapon or hard instrument in the struggle. The prisoners were all taken later in the day before Mr. J. Barton, at the Lymrn Police Court, when Meach gave evidence, which included the facts embodied in the above narrative. He said there were four guns against them, but only three were discharged. George Cook, under-keeper, said he had no firearms with him, nor had any of his party to his knowledge. When the poachers turned in their fight Willis pointed his gun at Witness's head, and pulled the trigger. Witness jumped aside, and heard the shot "whiz " past him. He then rushed at Willis, who struck him a heavy blow with the gun, but was overpowered. Ho had two pheasants in his pockets. When he fired witness was some eight yards away, but Ford was nearer, being in advance of all his companions. John Austin, under keeper at Arley, said that when be had nearly caught Perrin the latter turned round and fired at him. The gun was pointed at witness's head, and be only himself saved by rapidly stooping, hearing the shot go over his head. P.S. Harrington said that the prisoners were brought to the lock-up between four and five o'clock that morning. After hearing the statements of the keepers, he charged them all three with night poaching, being armed with guns, on the estate of Colonel Legh. All admitted the charge, adding "Worse luck." Witness aftewards charged them with in- tending to murder the watcher Ford, and Willis replied, "I put up my gun to save myself. A big youngfellow (Cook) took hold of my gun. We struggled for it and it went off. We never struck a blow." The prisoners were then jointly charged, with the wilful Murder of Janion. Willis said, "I am not guilty of wilful murder;" Perrin replied, "I can't see how it could be done except through this bother ;" and the third prisoner replied, "I cannot see that we murdered him. I have nothing else to say." Witness received two broken guns from the keepers,„and produced a perfect one, I which Willis had claimed as his. Hitchin identified another gun as his property, which was still loaded. On this evidence the prisoners were remanded until Friday next. The desperate character of the affair has created in- tense excitement in the district, and a full investigation of the circumstances is eagerly awaited. The inquest on Janion was opened on Tuesday, at Northytich, by Mr. 11. C. Yates, coroner for that division of Cheshire. The prisoners have been removed for safe keeping to Knutsford gaol.

THEFT OR A WATCH AT FARNWORTH STATPata.--John Watson, a respectably-dressed young man, described Ite a tinsmith, and 19 years of age, was indicted for having, at Widnes, on the 16th September, 1881, feloniously robbed one William Henry Lovelady, and stolen from his person one gold watch and chain, of the value of £45. Also unlaw- fully assaulted the said William Henry Lovelady, with intent feloniously to steal one gold watch and chain, the property of the said William Henry Lovelady.—Mr. M'Con- nell conducted the prosecution; the prisoeer was unde- feuded,—Mr. William Hy. Lovelady, a licensed victualler, residing in Liverpool, on being sworn, said he was seated in the train at Farnworth station on the occasion. The prisoner came in with a number of persons, and immediately he felt a tug at his watch chain, Watson having passed him the moment before. On looking down he noticed that his watch was out of his pocket and in the hand of the prisoner, but still attached to the chain, which was hooked to his waist- coat. Having got hold of him he called for the police, and Constable Hindle came forward, and the prisoner was taken into the stationmaster's office, where the prosecu- tor charged him. He was then formally handed over to the civil authorities. The value of the watch and chain was £45.--Prosecutor, in reply to the accused, said it was the stationmaster who first came to his assistance. He (prose- cutor) told the stationmaster that there were two women with the accused on the occasion. He did not see the women after he (the prosecutor) accused the prisoner, nor did he accuse one of them of stealing the watch. The watch was left in charge of the police.—William Henry Hindle, a constable employed by the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee, was examined. He saw the prosecutor on the occasion having hold of the prisoner. Witness also took hold of prisoner, who opened his hand, and the prosecutor took his wale; from it. On charging prisoner in the stationmaster's office he said, "You cannot charge me with stealing the watch, but with attempting to steal it. —Arthur Robinson, sergeant of the county police, to whom see prisoner was given in charge, was examined, and cc-, robor- ated the evidence of the , previous witnesses.—Ors Honour charged the jury in a few words, and the latter immediately returned a verdict of stealing the watch, and the prisoner was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment. CONCERT AT HITYTON. On Monday a concert was given in the Huyton and Roby schools, Damhouie-lane, Huyton, in aid of the funds of Huyton Quarry Branch of the Church of England Temper ance Society. The Rev. Canon Penshyn, vicar of Huytons presided, and the house was well filled. The artistes were: Mrs. Moss (Huyton), Miss L. James (Runcorn), Mr. George Barton (St. Helens), Mr. Tate, Mr. Vickery, and Mr. Geo. Bernard (Huyton), assisted by the St. Helens Glee Club, in- cluding Mr. Barton, solo pianoforte and accompanist, Miss M. E. Johnson, of Rainhill. The programme, on the whole, was a good one, and evidently appreciated by all. The con- cert commenced with the glee "Soldiers' love" (Kucken) by the St. Helens Glee Club, after which Mr. George Ber- nard, who has on several occasions assisted at concerts in connection with the temperance society, sang with much spirit Loder's song of "The diver," and was loudly applauded.. The gentleman possesses a tolerably powerful bass voice and uses it to fairly good advantage. Mrs. Moss rendered with sweetness and expression "At the ferry " (Willings); which was followed by the duet "The sailor sighs" (Smart) by Miss James and Mr. Barton. Finsuti's solemn and pathetic song, "The bugler," was given by Mr. Vickery„, which was succeeded by a pleasing solo on the pianoforte, entitled "Pasquinade ' (Gottschalk), by Miss Johnson, who ably sustained the reputation she had earned in the district as a remarkably good pianist. Miss James obtained a warm recognition in her rendering of the song "The better land (Cowan), and the same may be said of Mr. George Tate in his song "Thou art passing hence" (Sullivan). The chief feature of the evening was, however, the singing of Mr. Bar- ton, who was in excellent voice. His first contribution was the seranade, "Farewell, farewell, my mountain life " (Hatton), which he sang in his usual masterly style, and at the conclusion he was vocifeSously applauded, and in re- sponse he gave" Madaline," which was likewise keenly ap- preciated by the audience. The catch, entitled Mr. Speaker," by the club, which calmed roars of laughter, brought the first part of the programme to a close, and in the interval the Rev. A. T. Warne addressed the meeting. Re, remarked that they thaught that a fitting opportunity to ex- plain the objects of the society, towards whose funds the proceeds 9f that entertainment were to be devoted. They could notfail to be aware, he was quite sure, of the existence In the parish of an organization having for its aim" the lessening, if possible, of the dread I curse of drunkenness, which was so rife in their midst, especially after its first year's successful work at Ruyton Quarry. He then explained at length the scope and basis of the Church of England Temperance Society's operations. The concert wa& then proceeded with, the first item being the glee, "Banish, oh, maiden," (Lorenz); which was fol- lowed by Elliott's "Song of Hebrias," by Mr. Vickery. Miss James was successf al in securing the loud plaudits of the audience in her finished rendering of "The sparrow's ditty," (Archer). The combined sweetness and power of Mr. Barton's voice, with his felicity of execution, were strik- ingly exemplified in Bishop's beautiful song, "The pilgrim 01 love," (which he sang by desire), and he received that spontaneous outburst of applause so seldom accorded to the artistes, and he then sang "The maid of Llangollen." After the duet, "When the wind blows" (Smart), by Mrs. Moss and Mr. Vickery, and the song," Let me love thee" (Aditi), had been given, Mr. G. Bernard was loudly encored for his excellent rendition of Adam's song, " Midshipmite," and substituted "Jack's yarn." The sere- na adnen,e ' r', Slumber, sweetly slumber." by the glee club, brought a Very excellent and successful concert to close. A vote of thanks was passed to the artistes for their services, and the National Anthem was sung. A number of persons joined the society, including the Rev. G. J. Banner and Mr. Ed. B and others.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1881. TERRIBLE POACHING AFFRAY IN CHESHIRE. ONE MAN KILLED AND SEVERAL INJURED. Early on Monday nlorning 'a mosValeplorable occtirrenke happened near the village of Higll Legh, • a few miles from Lymm. cheshire. A melee there took place between a gang of poaehere anti a numbeiof keepers, with the result of almost immediate death to one man and glorious injuries td others, The estate of Mr, Henry Cornwall "Leah includes the district of High Legh, and fringes the Northwich divi- sion of the county. Its covers and coppices are well stocked. With game of all. Itinds,, and for , some tie past garigs of poachers have made the estate their "happy hunt- ing geound;" prowling ..about its western •extremities in bodies of five and six, or more, well armed, and caring little for the ordinary staff of gamekeepers. To put a stop to these depredations became a matter of absolute necessity, and on Sunday night the head-keeper, Walter Meach, assembled a force of ieur under-keepers and sixteen "watchers," with which he proceeded to Fox's Cover, a well-known portion of the estate. There they concealed themselves and watched patiently until two o'clock on Monday morning, when several shots were beard in the cover. The head-keeper and his party were not provided with fire-arms, as it appears, or at any rate the men had received no orders from Meech to bring their guns with them. Hearing the shots, the leader of the expedition immediately concluded that poachers were about, and he divided his force, sending one half to the bottom of the wood and taking the remainder himself to another portion, thus completely blocking all chance of un- observed egress from the plantation. Soon afterwards the poachers discovered that their proceedings were observed, and one of them shouted "They (the keepers) are out; get on." Four men were then seen, in the strong moonlight, to leave the cover and make off at top speed across the fields in the direction of Arley Hall, Meach and his men taking up the chase in real earnest. Three extensive fields were crossed, and then Meech, with an underkeeper named Cook, shouted several times to the fugitives to lay down the guns, which they were perceived carrying, and surrender. A reply came back that they would not "give up," but would shoot the first man who came up to them. The pursuing force gradually gained on the poachers, and after another request from Meach to give up their guns had been responded to in the same way, an order was given to close with the men. On hearing these words the four poachers turned deliberately towards the keepers and pre- sented their guns. Three of them fired, failure of the cap on the nipple of the fourth gun being the only reason why that weapon was silent. One of the attacking party fell at the discharge, and shots were heard to whistle past others, the life of one man being probably saved only by the rapidity with which he " ducked "on seeing the muzzle of the gun pointed at his head. The keepers, allowing their opponents no time to re-load, fell upon them, and a fearful struggle took place, the poachers using their guns freely upon their adversaries. The relative strength of the parties was, of course, too disproportionate to render doubtful the issue of the fight, and ultimately the four men were all secured. Two of them were desperately injured, one being almost unconscious, and one of the watchers, named Ford, was also fearfully hurt, the whole of the lower part of his jaw having been torn away, apparently by a charge of shot. Several of his comrades bore evident traces of the despera- tion with which the poachers had resisted the capture. Taking the wounded men and their prisoners, the keepers proceeded to the farm of Mr. Owen, about a mile distant, and roused him from bed. Hearing how badly hurt some of the combatants were, Mr. Owen harnessed a horse to his trap, and having placed the wounded poacher, whose name had been ascertained as Joseph Janion, and Ford in the vehicle, he, accompanied by Meech, set off for Northwich, where the nearest doctor resided. On the way Janion got worse, was very restless, and asked to be "turned round" several times, in order to ease his pain. Meech supported him on his arm, and did as desired. The wounded man said at last, "I am going to die; give me your hand; I have broken a blood vessel." Almost immediatly after he strug- _

PRESENTATION TO THE REV. C. F. MERIIIRGEN, ST. HELENS. On Monday evening, a very interesting presentation took [Lilac/fin the pt. Helens Town aJi. Thok Rae. C. F. 111ep;- " ' • margen, whothas now discharged the utiea devolving upon him as curate of the St. Helens Parish Church, is about to / • leave this town for Bristol, and on Sunday evening last the rev. gentleman preached his farewell sermon in the above church to a crowded congregation. His friends . being anxious that he should take away with him some token of their esteem, at once set to work, and their efforts culmina- ted in a substantial present being given to him on Monday night. There were present in the Council Chamber :—The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Miss Harrison, Rev. IL R. Moore, Rev. Mr. Topham, Dr. Garton, ,Mr. Brewis (town clerk), Alderman Mcßryde, Major and Mrs. Winclas and party, Major Willcocks (21st L.R.V.), Captain White, Mr, John Green, Mr. William Gamble, Mr. William Brooker (hon. treasurer), Mr. R. W. H. Thomas' and Mr. J. 11. Craik (hon. sees.), Miss Craik,, Mrs. Hart, Messrs. John 'Kitchen, Superintendent 'Johnston, Inspector Wood, Mr. B. A. Dmm-_ goole, Mr. Critchley, Mr. Ogden, Mr. George Itysley, Mr. H. Swift and party, Mr. C. C. White, Mr. John Fidler, Mr. D. M. F. Gaskin and Miss Gaskin, Mr. Urmson and Miss Urm- son, Miss Geskell and party, the Misses Halton, Mr. John Rimmer, Miss Gorst, Mr. and Mrs, Robert Cook, the Misses Morris, Mrs. Isaac Smith and Miss Taylor, Mr. Willgoose, Mr. Peter and Mrs. Greenough, Mr. and Mrs. W. J. Wright, Mr. A. C. C.arr, Mr. d. Moore, Mr. J. Bernard, Mr. Newbold, Mr. Jas. Grace, Mr. Jessie Boydell, and Mr. M. Hammill. Mr. J. H. CRAIK read a letter from Canon Carr, dated Brighton, which said—" I see you are bound by circum- stances: As to leaving, I sincerely hope you will change for the better in all respects. I shall miss your ever ready help and loyalty to the interests of the Church and myself; so will very many your untiring efforts for them. I only hope your successor will fill your place and study my wishes as you have always done. It is a matter of satisfac- tory reflection to us both that no breach has marred our Intercourse for seven years." The Rev. R. J. Ward wrote— "l am very sorry that an engagement this evening will pre- vent me from accepting your kind invitation to be present at the presentation of a testimonial to Mr, Mermargen. I should have been glad to have testified by my presence my heartfelt appreciation of his personal worth and ser- vices." .
The Mavorthen handed the purse and addrese to -

The Rev. C. F. MERMARGEN, who, in replying, said he was quite sure they would not think it affectation when he said he had not words to express his feelnigs on that occasion. He had not words to express the gratitude he felt for the generous present just presented to him. It would be absurd for him to say that such a large sum of money was of little value to him, but of not less value were the sentiments in which that presentation had originated. It would give him great moral support on his way. A clergy- man's duties might, perhaps, appear to be lighter than the duties of one who laboured physically hard ; but they were no means light, when there was taaen into consideration the many disappointments one met with when trying to eradi- cate some evil or bringing about some necessary reform. To have worked in the town—though with much weakness, many failures, and mourning over many disappointments—. and to have at last the words of generous sympathy, such unmerited—he might say—support extended to him, would be of very great value and support to him in the future. Wherever he went, whatever might be his future experi- ence, his life and action, he should never forget the generosity, kindness, and sympathy, which, not only now, but during the seven years and six months which expired on the let November, he had experienced amongst them. He had met with the kindness of all classes during thesperiod he had been in St. Helens. True, he had been amongst the poor, for when he entered the Church it was to go out as a missionary. And if work among the poor did invite trials, it had also its certain slue rewards. He had been on terms of intimate friendship with those who held views different to his own, and he did not think he could be accused of having made any compromise, for he and his friends had all strongly defended their particular views. They could not do very often as they could like. Having been in that diocese now for nine years, they would easily believe that on going into an entitely new diocese, and amongst an en- tirely new people, the moral support derived from their expression of kindness would be of the greatest use to him (Applause).

Dear sir,— As the representatives of a committee formed for the purpose of giving effect to a general desire expressed by our fellow townsmen that on leaving St Helens you should carry away some testimonial of the high esteem and the great admira- tion with which you are regarded, we beg you will accept the accompanying purse containing £l2O subscribed, not by your parishioneers alone, but also by many members of other religious bodies. THE RISE AND PROGRESS OF THE TEMPERANCE REFORMATION (Warrington: P. T. Winskill).—This is a subscription issue of a comprehensive history of the Temperance Reformation from the earliest period to the year 1881, by P. T. Winskill, dedicated to Dr. R. B. Grindr.al, one of the first medical men in the country to adopt and publicly advocate total abstinence principles, the founder of the first bond file total abstinence society in England. Mr. Winskill's work is re- plete with a vak fund of very interesting information which must have entailed a great expenditure of time in the col- lation. The facts thus presented are well worthy of being carefully perused by all interested in the progress of temper- ance and the stemming of the tide of intemperance. Whilst the author has principally dealt with the United 'Kingdom, he has given a brief resume of the operations in other coun- tries. Probably it may be thought by some that the ailthor might have devoted more space to the work of many of the societies, and when giving the history of the formation of societies and the holding of meetings, ft would have been just as interesting if all the names of those present had not been given but simply those who took an actiVe part or rather the most prominent part therein, and thus have left space for details of a more, general interest. Altogether; however, we think the author hss performedlhis flit-imposed task in a manner which reflects credit upon himself, whilst his industry and perseverance cannot but be admired by every temperance man. The work is one which will no doubt be rightly regarded as a book of reference, and we commend it as worthy of a place in every household. We notice that the work contains a very pleasing reference to the formation of the Warrington Temperance Society, which must be of great interest to Warringtonians and to which we may probably refer on a future occasion. Amongst those who have subscribed for copies of the work we notice Messrs. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Peter Rylands, M.P., Arthur Pease, M.P., B. Whitworth, M.P., John Crostield, J.P., E. Milner, J.P., S. Rigby, J.P., J. Rylands, J.P. Rev. C. E. Carleton, Rev. R. Pilcher, Rev. J. Warnock, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. J. Yonge, the Mayor of Huddersfield, the Mayor of Clitheroe, dm.
