NEW BAPTIST CHAPEL, EARLES.; TOWN. OPENING SERVICES.

The aphorism that " From small beginnings great results may come" was exemplified on Monday, when the Rev. El:Stowell Brown, of Liverpool, opened the firelvehapei in Earlestewn belonging to the Baptist •denomination. It is ten years since a few earnest men opened a small room in Market-street for public worship according to the principles . . of the Baptists; and from that time to the present their numbers have been increasing. 'Finding the accommodation insufficient, it was was decided to make an effort to build a chapel. In April last the first visible result of this effort was the laking the foundation stone of the chapel, and the completion of which was celebrated on Monday with much ,enthusiasm. The chapel is built with ,grey Garston bricks, with red pressed brick dressings, and red 'end blue string courses. The main building occupies an area of 54 feet by 33, and at the back is a large class room 31 by 15 feet, and two smallvestries. The design is Gothic, and viewed from the road the chapel has a very pretty appearance. At the entrance to the building is a small vestibule. Then passing through folding doors, with stained lead light glass panels, the body of the chapel is reached, which will accommodate 300 persons. In the centre are open benches, whilst down each side are ordinary forms with reversible backs. The windows are made of small lead lights, each pane having the shape of a diamond. The rostrum and communion are made of pitch pine, artistically carved, and the minister's chair is of a quaint but pretty pattern. The whole of the furniture is made of pitch pine. Behind the rostrum are three recesses in the wall ornamented with Gothic heads. Although these are at present empty, it is proposed to place in them texts from scripture in illuminated capitals. The baptiatry is formed under the communion, and is lined with white and red tiles. The place is efficiently ventilated by Tobin's patent inlet tubes fixed in the bottom of each win- dow, and on the roof is placed one of Boyle's extractors. The hot water small tube system is used for beating the chapel, and light is obtained from two chandeliers. The architect is Mr. G. F. Aveling, a member of the congrega- tion, and the work was carried out by Mr. E. Davies, builder, Earlestown. Mr. John Starkie had the contract for the plumbing and gas fittings. At the opening service the chanel was well filled, many local ministers being present. The Rev. H. Stowell Brown selected for his text the 2nd v. 2c. of the Ist Epistle to the Corinthians, "For I determined not to know anything among you save Jesus Christ and him crucified." At the conclusion of along sermon, he gave a few particulars of the financial position of the church. He said the building and furniture had cost £1,150, towards which £775 had been received in money and promises. Of that sum £486 had been provided by the Earlestown friends, and £2BB 10s. by friends in Liverpool. A debt of £375 thus remained. He need not say anything about the structure; for it must have commended itself to all that had seen it. He did not think anyone could say that the place was dear, or that there had been any extravagance in its construction. They hoped to considerably diminish the debt by the open- ing services, so that in a short time they might rejoice in having a place of worship entirely free from such encum- brance. He was pleased to see the large number of friends present that afternoon. It was indicative of sympathy with the movement, which he and not a few in Liverpool had sympathised with irons the beginning. A collection was then made which realised about £2O. An excellent tea had been provided in the class-room for those persons who had come from a distance, and it was partaken of by a con- siderable number. In the evening a publid meeting was held in the Chapel, uider the presidency of the Rev. H. Stowell Brown. There was again a good attendance' and amongst those present were the Revs. G. M. W. Carey, 141. A., D. Jones, and S. Hawkes, of Liverpool; W. Pilling, Hill Cliffs ; J. Allatt, W. C. Tayler, of Earlestown ; Mr., J. C. Farnie, Liverpool ; and Councillor Wallington, Warrington. Letters of apology had been received from the Rev. H. Hall, Wigan, Mr. W. P. Lockhart, Liverpool, and the Rev. M. Dickenson, of Earles- town.

The Rev. W. C. TAYLER said it seemed only proper that he should lay before the friends gathered there a few things as touching those for whom that house had been built, and touching the house itself. A public announcemPnt made , prior to October 22nd, 1871, acquainted the Earlestown public that a body of Christians called Baptists intended to open an upper room in Market-street for public worship of almighty God. Before that date Baptists as a corporate body had no existence in Earlestown. Then some five Individuals who before had but little cohesion were united together in one body and for one purpose. If success went for anything, then the present Rosition and future prosperity of that infant cause affirmed that the five individuals before mentioned had acted wisely and well in what they did. (Hear, hear.) At the commencement of their labours the Baptist denomination was represented by five persons and their families. At the close they found a church member- ship of 40, a congregation of 120,a Sunday school of over 200 ohildren—(hear,bear)—and a house of prayer, of which neither their kihd fostering mother, Myrtle-street Church, nor the Earlestown public need be ashamed. (Applause.) They felt grateful that they had such a building to present to the father of their spirits, and this prayer was that in the greatness of His condescension He will accept that which they had dedicated to Hint that day and fill it now and evermore with His presence and glory. Their future pros- pects were certainly not dark. They had the esteem and respect of sister denominations. It was not surely out of place to mention two pleasing facts to prove this. Mr. Crozier, the esteemed resident minister, in announcing their opening services, very kindly pressed his people to be present. Their good friends the Primitive Methodists had put off a missionary service until the next day that they I might be present there. The had a number of young people in the Sunday school who had been with them from the first and who were deeply attached to the cause. (Hear, hear.) Several outsiders bad expressed their intention to join them. It might be that some would ask " Who are you 1"" To such, if such there were, they were by no means loth to reply. They were Christians, followers imperfect, certainly, of the Christ. They believed in the Father's infinite and glorious love to them ; that those who had been redeemed by the Son should be united together in holy and sweet fel- lowship. Christ was their only Lord ; His laws were only to be obeyed. They believed that this world, so defaced by sin, had been given by the Father to the Son. But they were not only Christians ; they were immersed Christians; holding that it was the will of Christ that everyone who repented of sin should be immersed in water, that thereby there should be set forth death unto sin, and a resurrection into holiness. That would suffice as to themselves. To the members of the congregation that day would be a day of days. They had before them a tangible and not-to-be-mistaken answer to their prayers. The gift of God as much so as though, like Jonah's gourd, he had caused it to grow up out of the earth. To Him they gave their sincere thanks. The thought of the building had existed almost as soon as they commenced to exist. When they were not three years Old £5 Os. was placed in. the bank towards that, building. That sum was the out- spoken determination of the friends to have the chapek. From that day efforts more or less energetic were put forth, and now they stt.w the result. It was a good result, though they had tv.t all they could wish and really wanted. At present they would have to carry on the Sunday school in the chapel. They had the ground for a school and all they ' wanted was the money, and certairly they would not say nay to anyone who might offer it to them, lie then spoke of the help they had received from the Chairman and other friends, and especially complimented Mr. Avelint; for his work in connection with the building, concluding with giving the financial statement read by the preacher in the afternoon. Mr. George McCorquodale and Messrs. Evans and Co. had each given £2O; the Sunday school scholars bad contributed £32 Is. 2d.,—(applause)—and collected Di 12s. 9d. (Applause.) a The CHAIRMAN said he yielded to no one present in his appreciation of the work which had been done by their Earlestown friends under the direction of Mr. Aveling. He was snrprised to find, for so small a. sum of money, so ex- cellent a piece of work, and adapted to the' requirements of the congregation which they expected would meet within those walls. He had from the first taken great interest in this undertaking, as it was fitting he should do, because the members of that church were members of • Myttle-street church, Liverpool, and the:charch was one of its branches. And one of the branches be had taken great pleasure in Icontemplatine, for he thought that it had done quite as ,-rmteirgood and given them less trooble than some places that they had been acquainted with. (Laughter.) The prospects of the new church were encouraging in every way,. and it was pleasing that the members had done so much among themselves. (Near, hear.) They must feel :especial pleasure in seeing the work completed, and have a greater interest in the chapel. There was hardly anybody Iliving who contributed anything to the building of the , chapel in Liverpool. He wondered that the people took so much interest in it. They had had it given to them, and it was not well for people to have chapels given to them any more than it was good for people to have bread and cheese given to them. (Laughter.) A child might have ,too much of a mother's blessing; and so might a church; and they had not been too indulgent to that church and did not mean to be. (Laughter.) This work was completed, but let the members bear in mind that their work was not com- pleted, and never would be. As long as they lived they were to seek an extension of the cause—(bear, hear) ;._which they all professed to love; for which they often prayed; and in the promotion of which all of them were taLru or less engaged. two things wanting to give completeness to the whole. They wanted a schoolroom and they would do well to put something in the bank towards the building of a minister's house. (Hear. hear.) That would ensure the residence of Mr. Taylor in the neighbourhood. The Church was one body called by different names, and in a population of 10,000 people there was plenty of work for them.a.ll to do, and they welcomed any place which in the broad spirit of the Gospel would help to win that neigh- bourhood for Christ (Hear, hear.) He was grieved to see the kind of literature that was read by a large proportion of the people. He wished they had a larger number purchas- ing our great English classics, and a decreasing number who could find nothing higher and better to read that the sport- ing papers. They wanted to raise the spiritual tone of the young men and maidens; of those engaged in Sunday school instruction; of commercial life, so that everything that was done should be done with a single eye to the honour and glory of God. The Rev. Datum, Jonas, secretary, of the Liverpool Baptist Union, congratulated them upon the erection of this house of worship. When they which had erected that building, or had caused it be erected, and they who had formed the church had passed away, the chapel would still remain a perennial stream of blessing to the world and the neighbourhood in which it was placed. None but God knew the good which came horst an effort like the one which they had that day completed.' He hoped they were not satisfied with what they had done, bat took it as an earnest of what they had to do in a still more difficult undertaking: He urged upon them the necessity of the work of bringing men and women to the Gospel of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The Rev. W. Prustsa (Hill Cliffe) congratulated them upon having secured such a commodious and beautiful chapel. He hoped they would be -much blessed in their work, that many precious souls would be torn again, and that they would have abundant cause to rejoice that they had been the means, in God's bands, in raising a building wherein to worship God. Mr. Pilling then advised i the members to be constant n their attendance at chapel ; be in time; be attentive to the ministration of your pastor; carefully read the work of God; and then they would not be what he was afraid many Christians in these days were, "surface Christians," but grounded in the truth, that they might,know what to believe, why they believed, and be able to give a reason for the hope that was within them. He should always be willing to accord his sympathy and help, and he hoped that in time they would have a Sunday school, and still cry "We want more room." (Applause.) The Rev. S. Some people were always talking of Heaven as being a place of rest. It would be, but he hoped it would also be a place of work and far better work than we were able to do here •, and our association with the Church should be one which produced good substantial work. He hoped all the members of the Church would be working members. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. G. M. W. Carey and other gentlemen then addressed the meeting.

At the York Assizes Joseph Taylor, a man about 507 ears old, was sentenced to penal servitude for life for lulling Mary Bowen, his niece, at Bradford. A reduction of from 10s. to 15s. per cwt. had to be sub- mitted to by sellers at the Chester cheese fair on Wednesday. Many dairymen took their stock home again. The decline is attributed to American importations. The Deanery of Carlisle has been bestowed upon the Rev. John Oakley, of St. Saviour's, Hoxton, a clergyman who has been labouring for 14 years as rector of a densely popu- lated parish in London, and who has by his broad and liberal sympathies secured a large amount of esteem amongst the working classes in the metropolis. LORD RANDOM CIDTRCHILL.-•-it is enough to make the late Lord Beaconsfield writhe in his grave to sea the fuss the Tory press are making over this unlinked cub of politics. If a once great pulitical party, respectable if mistaken, that is according to the point of view from which it may be re- garded—we speak impartially—have no better leader than this lively product of misapplied taxes, they had better pre- serve a dignified silence, and turn their "organs" into. literary and scientific journals.—Punch.

Ma Lams Dtsr sranusrrzn Cnunca.—One more piece of evidence showing that disestablishment has not injured the Irish Church. Addreasing the Clogher Diocesan Synod, the Archbishop of Armagh said:—" From the returns made by the Prienate and Bishops at the commencement of this century, and by comparing them with our Church as it now is, we tind that, disestablished as we now are, our state is very little worse and in some respects better, than it then was. . . . These are are all signs of advancement and prosperity, and if we could remain as we now are, we should do well." Canon Finlay also said that " it was a matter for deep thanful- uess to them all that their diocese was in such a satisfactory condition. They had got in the diocese a body of clergymen second to none, who were throwing themselves heart and soul into all the work." We commend the-se frank and manly utterances to croakers like Bishop %de, who thinks that Disestablisbment would "greatly weaken the Chnrcb, and almost destroy it, in the rural districts." What is possible for disestablished Protestantism in Ireland ought to be comparatively easy in England.—The Liberator THE Qtrzertorr or Disneranusinutzer in England is in a transition state. It has come to be pretty well understood, and it now excites no terror. Some Episcopalians have made up their minds to accept it, with resignation if not with cheerfulness. Others are busy shaking the Establish- ment to its foundations by their complaints and protests ; by their demands for organic changes, and by their affirmation of principles which, if they are eincere and earnest, must presently bring them to Disestablishment. Never was there such an abundance of materials at our command to illustrate the inexpediency and the mischievousness of legislation for the promotion of religion. Never have these opposed to us so played into our bands as they are doing at the present time, however unconsciously. That there must be some changes in the existing relations between Church and State is generally allowed; our business is to show that attempts to seriously modify, and to purify, the present system must certainly fail, and that Church reform must be the work of an emancipated Church, and not of a Legislature trying to give some relief to the Church, while adhering to the ancient traditions of State-craft.—The Liberator.

WIIIE CHVHCH PATRONAGE BILL DID NOT PASS. Dealing with the statement that Mr. Stanhope's Bill was defeated by Liber tionist obstruction, The Liberator says a The two assanytions on which the charge is based are— that the Church Patronage Bill was an unobjectional measure, and thar it was only the opposition of 'Liberators' which prevented its becoming law. The baselessness of the first assumption is shown by the objections which Church- men have taken to the Bill. Last month we quoted the decisive testimony of the Chairman of the Committee for abolishing purchase in the Church—a Churchman—and now we can point to the criticisms of members of, the various diocesan Conferences, of which we have given some report in another column. The discussions at these Conferences show, not only that Churchmen are quite divided in opinion as to the merits of Mr. Stanhope's Bill, but that they are in a confused state of mind in regard to the whole question. Mr. Stanhope himself admits that the Bill may be improved, and we expect that presently there will be expressions of 'satisfaction that neither of the Bills of 1881 became law. That the loss of the Bill is due to Mr. Illingworth, and those Who acted with him, is simply preposterous. They did no more than prevent the Bill being read a second time Without any discussion, or with a discussion not beginning till the small hours of the morning, and there was no other time available, and consequently the question shared the fate of dozens of other questions which had to be postponed till next sessicp." . 3RD ANNUAL SALE FOR THE ARTlSTS.—Organised in their be- half by the Secretary in London to the Belgian Commission of the International Exhibitions of 1871 to 1874. A collection of PICTURES and WATER-COLOUR DRAWINGS exceed- ing in excellence and variety the well-known collections of the two past years, and composed exclusively of the contri- butions of artists whose works are regularly admitted and sought after t the Royal Academy, the Paris Salon, and the leading exhibitions of England and the continent. The . pictures and drawings are of the highest standard of excel- lence, and many of the choicest and most remarkable works which have been seen in recent exhibitions are comprised in this collection. English artists are largely represented, and particular interest will be attracted to the great number of works in this section by men of rising fame. The conti- nental portion presents a rich variety, and many of the best known artists in Europe have contributed to it. The works in most instances are from the walls of important ex- hibitions, many being diploma pictures, which have either been honourably mentioned or have procured medals or other distinctions for their authors when exhibited in the Paris Salon, Berlin Academy, Belgian Government Exhibitions of Brussels and Antwerp,. the German Academies of Munich and Dusseldorf, Milan Exhibition, &c.--By MESSRS. BRANCH AND LEEPE, on WEDNESDAY, THURSDAY, and FRIDAY, the 18th, 17th, and 18th inst., at One o'clock each day, in the HANOVER ART GALLERIES, PICTURES and WATER-COLOUR DRAWINGS, forming ft most beautiful, interesting, and varied collection of over 400 works. The range of subject to• be found in the collection is almost unlimited. A large proportion consists of very fine figure pictures of historical, classical, • military, and other subjects ; exquisitely painted interiors; gems of genre painting in domestic and humourous subjects ; street scenes of present and past interest; landscapes of the most varied subjects, and representing. favourite Views in many of the wost interesting spots in Europe. The following are some of the principal pictures P. C. tailardi's humourous work, 'The Bachelors"; Ccessin's admirable picture from the Paris Salon, "A Pleasure Party in 1795 " • a beautiful poetical landscape by Henri Pleron, "Morn- ing Mists at Hurley-on-Thames ' ; W. Kreling's important figure-subject, "The Love Token " ; one of Carl Rodeck's grand forest sunsets: a line lake scene by A. Norman, "The Roma- dalliord, Norway ;" two excellent specimens of still life by Falcdetti ; "Episodes of the Franco-German War," by Chr. Sell; a grand work by J. Bauck, "A Moonlight Solitude ;" L. Hmtke's important picture, "The Heir to the Throne ;" a highly interesting work by A. Braith, and many equally im- portant pictures by the following well known artists H. Ten Kate J Canard F. Schmiechen E. de Schampheleer Charles Robertson Th. L. de Haas C. F. Phlippeau T. E. Duverger Leon Herbo Joseph Coomans A. Delobbe Thos Fyne L. Franz A. Corelli R. de Egusquiza E. J. Varley J. IL Wells F. talon Burton Barher A. Spring J. Frappa A. W. Strutt W. 0. Eddington P. de Coninck Muse Bianchi W. de Gegerfelt Brubk Lajos C. S. Lidderdale Gustave Bouvier Geoffroy Rolled Gallon A. Bonifazi Henri Motte H. Gqgarten F. Honig R. Burnier J. W. Smith Miss J. Macgregor J. Heydendahl J. J. Watson • Edwin Bale A. Olafsen Pio Bianchi J. Koppers A. Bodenmutter S. Morton Fisher Carl Schultze G. Months J'. A. Benwell J. Ballavoine L. Herrmann E. Farasyn Tristram Ellis , H. Oehrnichen H. Valkenburg Karl Daubigny H J. Burgers H. Bource Antony Serres E. Delperee T. Cereiez Ch. Soubre J. Cambain E. Salaruson A. Musin Paul Seignae The sale, as in former years, has been organised by the Secretary of the Belgian Commission for the late International Exhibitions at South Kensington, and in regard to the foreign section the fact that official assistance has been given by com- mittees of artists in the choice and selection of the works contributed, and that each picture in the collebtion is sent direct by the artist, affords the most ample guarantee to connoisseurs and the public. May be privately viewed by ticket on Saturday, the 12th instant, and publicly on Monday and Tuesday, the 14 and 15th instant, and catalogues had at Messrs. BRANCH and LEETE'S offices, Hanover-street, Liverpool.
By Mr. TH-031.18 SUTTOk

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1881.

shalled in his opening speech and proved by his wit- nesses, and which he reiterated with irresistible force in his closing address. The Lord Chief Justice in his summing up set the seal of his endorsement upon those cumulated proofs ; and the jury were so entirely convinced and thoroughly at one, that after a ten minutes' consultation they retutned the verdict of guilty. Lefroy may still protest .his innocence, but no one else questions the justice of the verdict and sentence. That an educated, intellectual young man like he is should have had no visible compunction in assailing with all the savagery of a wild beast an inoffensive old gentleman, and should have taken his life in such an awful manner, merely with the hope of picking his victim's pockets, is a startling example of the devilism which is dormant in some men's nature, under a respectable and quiet exterior. Lefroy is a most dangerous criminal, and it is well he did not make good his escape after the police let him go on the night of the murder.

RUNCORN RIGBY CILLRITY. —A few days ago, the distribution ef this well-known charity took place, in the presence of the Rev. Canon Barclay and Mr. John 'Brundrit, and 60 aged women were each presented with a flannel petticoat.

RuNconx Rim—This annual saturnalia passed off during the early days of the week, and attracted large num- bers of people, mostly of "the baser sort." Some of the in- habitants of the immediate neighbourhood loudly complain of the nuisance which they allege to be caused to them by the holding of the fair. SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES.—On Monday evening a service of song entitled "Home, Sweet Home," was given in the Oakland-street Wesleyan Sunday School, Widnes. Mr T. Robinson presided. The connective reedings were given by Mrs. Robinson and Mr. Whitley ac'ed as con- ductor to the choir. At the close collections were made on behalf of the trust fund.

WIDNES AND " TIIE FrFrH."—The fifth of Novem- ber passed off very quietly in Widnes. Nothing took place that is specially worthy of recording, and year by year the festival appears to be losing its attractiveness, thanks to the vigilance of the authorities. On Wednesday, at the Police Court, a dealer in fireworks was fined for selling them to a youth under age. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.—On Monday afternoon, a boatman named Samuel Theobold, of Lawton, Stafford- shire,l was assisting to unload his boat of crates in the Francis Dock, when the grapnels connected with one of them•become detached, and the heavy crate fell from a con- siderable height upon him, seriously injuring him. Dr. Mauritz is now in attendance upon the poor fellow.

„ I MiNTERTAINMENT AT 11IINCOEN.—An entertainmet ! was given on Monday night, at the Mersey Mission room Runcorn, the proceeds of which are intended for the purchase of material to be made up for the bazaar to be held in Dec. Mr. Robert Norman was in the chair, and there was a very fair attendance. An interesting programme was gone through ny Misses Rhodes, Wright, Edwards, Foulkes, and Messrs. Morris, Pixton, Saunders, and Edwards. The piano used was kindly lent by Mr. Ellison. Guy Few= DAY AT RUNCORN. —This festival ap- pears year by year to be less observed in Runcorn district, and will, probably, in time pass into desuetude altogether. This year the Commissioners issued a large number of notices which seemed to have the very happy effect of making the youthful portion of the community more cautious as to how and where they carried out their pranks, and thus the efforts of the police to preserve the public from any avoidable annoyance were ably seconded.

HILTON PAROCHIAL CLOTHING SOCIETY.— (Founder Sir Richard Brooke, Baronet).—The annual distribution of clothing took place on the afternoon of the 4th inst., the Rev. J. Lockwood, presidinE,t, who gave a suitable address to the members. Lady Brooke, as honorary secretary, was also preseut, and spoke some words of counsel and encouragement. The number of members for the past year was 173, and the subscriptions, including bonus, amounted to £lO3 7s. 6d.

• -•— -- A IturtconN STABLE ON FlRE..—Shortly after seven o'clock on Monday morning, a fire broke out in a stable Owned by Mr. John Richardson, butcher, of Church-street, in Canal-street. There was a large quantity of straw and three horses in the building which was two storeys high. These animals were fortunately taken out before they were injured. When the firemen arrived with the reel and hose, un ter the command of Superintendent Wright, the whole structure was enveloped in flames. The fire was however got under in a short time. There were three stacks near, which must have been burnt down but for the promptitude with which the fire brigade were at the fire. The building which was almost completely destroyed, is insured with the Phcenis Insurance Company. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—L,ZNCORN BRANCH.— On Sunday, two sermons will be preached in St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn, by the Rev. John Kilner, of London, one of the general secretaries of the parent society, and formerly missionary in Ceylon. Mr Kilner has a high reputation as a speaker, and no doubt the beautiful edifice will be I crowded. In the afternoon the Sunday schools will assemble in the gallery of St. Paul's, and will be addressed by the Rev. Peter Hargreaves, returned missionary from South Africa. The rest of the building will be reserved for adults. The annual meeting will take place on Monday evening, and the proceedings, which will be presided over by Mr. Joseph Cooke, of St. Helens, will commence at seven o'clock.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Sunday an accident of a serious nature happened to a man named Bernard Fallon, the Superintendent of the vitriol department at Messrs. Pilkington's chemical works, Widnes. About nine o'clock, he ascended a stage erected over some tanks con- taining sulphuric acid, for the purpose of shutting off one of the taps near the cistern. He stepped on a plank which lay between the steps and the spot where the taps were, when it gave way, and he fell about five feet into the sulphuric acid. His cries brought several men to the spot, who lifted him out, washed him with hot water, and took him to the hospital, where he was attended by Dr. O'Keeffe. The poor fellow was burned and scalded in a dreadful manner, and it was at first feared be would lose his sight, but we under- stand he is now progressing favourably. TUE DEATII OF A Ruivconx AUCTIONEEI3.—The remains of Mr. John Mack. auctioneer, of Runcorn, who died a few days ago, was interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Monday afternoon, in the presence of numerous friends. The procession left deceased's residence, High-street, about half-past two, and the hearse was preceded by a large number of tradesmen. In the first mourning coach were the Rev. Canon Carelay and Dr. McDougall, in the second Mr. Mack (brother of the deceased), Mr. George Mack (brother of deceased), Mr. George Mack (son of deceased). and three grandsons; and in the third coach were Messrs. John Frod- sham, John Rayner, and John Leicester. The funeral ser- vice was conducted by the Vicar, and the funeral arrange- ments were carried out by Mr. Henry Randle of Bridge. Street. Mr. S. Yarwood supplied the hearse and mourning coaches. The deceased formerly lived at Liverpool, and had for many years occupied a position as auctioneer and stationer in Runcorn. He was a very quiet, inoffensive man.

Speaking of Runcorn the document says that the work during the year has been as follows :—Visits to boatmen in their hous-s, flats, and ships, 6,092 ; persons addressed, 10,614: meetings, 208 ; attendance, 11,610; Sunday schools, 188 ; attendance, 10,280; open air meetings, 25; attendance, 2:260; parish church, 2,749; day and night schools, 27; attendance, 386: pledges, adults and children, 150; Band of Hope and tem- perance meetings. 37; attendance, 2,525; mothers' meetings, 30; attendance, 459. These facts reflect much credit upon Mr. Shaw. the indefatigable missionary of the Runcorn branch, for whom it is proposed to build a residence. The movement has been taken up with much heartiness, and gives every promise of succeeding.. , RUNCORN Bunrer. BOAR.D.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. Coleburn presided, and there were also present—Messrs. Thomas Norman, James Handley, Wm. Littler, G. Moss, and W. P. Salkeld (secretary). The report showed that tho interments for the mouth ending October 25th were 15 ; corresponding month last year, 24: decrease, 9. The receipts from March 25 to October 25,were £l3O 17s. 4d., and for the corresponding period last year £146 Os., making a decrease of £l5 88. Bd.--Mr. James Handley read the report of the special meeting of the Finance Committee, which stated that it had been resolved that in order to pay off the mortgage of £950, falling due in De- cember next, the following sums be borrowed :—£4oo from the " Lily of the Valley" Lodge of the Order of Oddfellows, repayable in four annual instalments of £lOO each, com- mencing on the 14th of December, 1888; £3OO from the "Duke of Devonshire" Lodge, repayable in three annual in- stalments of £lOO, commencing December 14, 1892; £lOO from the " Earl of Chester" Lodge, repayable on the 14th of December, 5P5;1 and that the balance be paid out of the sinking fund account. They further recommended that two precepts be at once issued on the overseers for payment of £240—namely, £l2O on sinking fund and £l2O to meet cur- rent expenses.—The secretary stated that Mrs. Bibby and Captain Millinger thanked the Burial Board for the care and attention they paid to everything connected with the ceme- tery, and especially for having replaced the glass shades which had been broken by a youth named James M'Turk

div.p: EAELESTOWN, WIDNES, AND NEWTON BIIILDTNO SO- CIETY.-Mr. Carlile and Mr. Midwood, both of Widnes, have been appointed stewards of this society.

ACCIDENT AT Ru:worm Docxs.—On Monday a bag of oats fell upon a man named Simon Hopkins, as the steamer Elaugh Castle was being unloaded at Runcorn docks, and broke one of his legs. HALTOI•I MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —At the meeting of this society on Monday the Rev. J. Bateman presided, and Mr. S. Barrow read a paper on "Farmers' Grievances." Messrs. T. Miller, A. E. Davies, G. Penning- ton, B. Haddock, and J. Baguley were amongst the speakers in the discuss:on which afterwards followed.

BRUNSWICK BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.-011 Tuesday night the first meeting of this Band of Hope took place at the school, Brunswick-street, Mr. T. Norman presided. A very interesting programme was gone through, which in- cluded songs, recitations, and glees. During the evening, Mr. Simpaon, superintendent of the school, delivered a capital address. ROCK SAVAGE PRIMITIVE METHODlSTS.—Anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday, at the Rock Savage Farm, (Mr. Stokes'), by Mr. Thomas Stringfellow and Mr. James Dobson. There were large congregations, and the collections realised £5. On Monday, the children belonging to the Mission were treated to tea. During the afternoon they were allowed to play in a neighbouring field,where they ran races for prizes. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY—On Monday evening a meeting was held in the girls' schoolroom, Halton, in view of forming a society for the winter months. The Rev. J. Lockwood occupied the I chair. It was decided that a debating class would be the most beneficial, and it was proposed by Mr. D. Baguley, and seconded by Mr. Lambert, that the Vicar open the session with an essay on Monday evening next. This he consented to do. It was proposed by Mr. Fandy, and seconded by Mr. M. Leach, that Mr. R. Fryer be appointed hon. secretary, Which was carri cd. THE MADRIGAL CLUB'S FIRST CONCERT.—The first concert of the Runcorn Madrigal Club of the present season is Haydn's greatest oratorio " The Creation," and will take place on the 21st inst. at the Public Hall. Year by year this society grows under their excellent conductor, Mr. Argent, in popular favour. The resources of the society on the present occasion will be fully drawn upon, and, judging from past experience they will prove sufficient for the rendition of the oratorio with more than an average degree of excellence. The society has lately been augmented by a band.

A CATHOLIC PRIEST FINED FOE I3EING DRONE AT PRESCOT.-At the Prescot l'olice Court on Saturday, Patrick Edward Byrne, who said he was a Catholic priest from Dublin (and who was attired as such), was charged with being drunk. On the previous evening the prisoner was found drunk and disorderly near the Catholic Chapel, Prescot, by a number of young men, who took him to the police office. Prisoner was very boisterous in the police office and cursed and swore very hard. As the prisoner had nowhere to go nor any money in his possession, he was locked up for safety. A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted, but as he could not pay he was committed for seven days.

TIIE PROPOSED COUNTY COURT FOR WlDNES.—Within the last few days Mr. W. T. llusband, solicitor, of Widnes, has written to Sir R. A. Cross reminding him that he i•ave him permission to address him on the subject, in case nothing was heard in regard to the matter by November. No intimation had been received as to the fate of the peti- tion, and he should be obliged if Sir R. A. Cross could as- certain anything in regard to it. The following is Sir R. A. Cross's reply:—" Eccle Riggs, Broughton-in-Furness, No- vember 9th, 1881.—Dear Sir,—l have this day written to the Lord Chancellor on the subject of your letter yesterday. I have no doubt his serious illness has prevented him from taking any steps.—Faithfully yours, R. A. Crtoss.—Mr. W. T. Husband, Widnes."

BUILDING SOCIETY MEETING AT RUNCORN.—The annual meeting of the shareholders of the United Cheshire and Lan- cashire Permanent Benefit Society and Savings Fund, of which Mr. T. Simister is President, was held in the Trinity School room, Runcorn, on Thursday night. There was a good at- tendance. The eighteenth annual report which was read stated that the committee had had to decline opportunities for good investments in consequence of the receipts being required to meet withdrawals. The amount available for dividends was £2,176. 12s. 7d„ out of which it was proposed to pay a dividend of 4 per cent., which will absorb £1,741. 3s. 7d., leaving a balance of £435. 9s. Od. Flom this sum £162. 2s. Sd. will be carried to the reserve fund, as specified in the rules, and the balance £273. Gs. 4d. to next year's accounts. The assets amounted to £48,946. is. 5d., including the amount due on properties forfeited to the society, and which have, recently been valued by an ex- perienced builder, at £1,003. ss. Od. more than the remount due on them to the society. The liabilities are £43,514 6s. 2d, showing a balance in favour of the society of £5,431. 15s. 3d. After paying the dividend proposed, there will be a In trgin of £3,690. us. Bd. to meet any loss that may be sustained. A vote of confidence in the officers of. the society was pro- posed by the Rev. Canon Barclay. secfnded by the Rev. W. Preston, and carried unanimously. A general feeling was expressed in the manner in which the society's affairs had been managed during the year.—The retiring officers were all re-elected.

WIDNES PARISII CHURCH SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENT.— The second of the series of entertainments on behalf of the Parish Church schools took place on Tuesday. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes, presided. The concert opened with the glee "A Spring Song," which the glee class gave with a correctness which speaks well for their careful training and vocal abilities. Three other pieces were given by the glee class "Glorious Apollo," "Oh Nanny, wilt thou Gang we' Me," and " The Song of the Brotherhood." The two last mentioned deserve special praise. Mrs. James White gave" Somebody's coming "very effectively, and Mr. T. Davies, a popular local vocalist, rendered "Life is a River" in a manner which elicited an encore. Mrs. Wright-Williams gave "What will you:do, love?" and was heartily applauded. By his rendering of "The Bloom is on the Rye"—one of the most beautiful modern songs in the vocalist's repetoire, Mr. I. B. Imison, who did full justice to the piece, won a hearty encore, and an equally favourable reception was accorded to Mr. Unison's second song, "As I'd nothing else to do." Mrs. James White gave the song " Gentle Words," with taste and feeling. Mr. T. Davies sang "Fifty Miles under the Sea," the humorous nature of the latter evidently giving genuine amusement to the audience, both being encored. Miss Lord gave a pianoforte solo, "The Bdttle March of Delhi," and was encored. The entertainment was varied by the introduction of two humorous readings. One from Lover's well-known Irish novel, "Rory O'More," and the second Mrs. Candle's curtain lectures, by Mr. W. Treacy, jun. The concert was not quite so well attended as the excellent programme prepared would have led one to expect. But the thinly filled benches may probably be accounted for by the fact of its being the same week of the St. Ambrose C hurch bazaar.

RUNCORN NEWTOWN MISSION Curacx.—On Wednesday a tea party was held in Newtown Mission Room, Runcorn. The room was prettily decorated with flags and banners be- longing to the Sabbath school. About 100 persons sat down to a substantial tea. After tea a miscellaneous entertain- ment took place, over which the Rev. Canon Barclay pre- sided.—The Chairman said that it was the duty of all con- cerned in the matter to askthemselves what was the object of the mission ? It had been defined as "the multiplication of spiritual machinery." Its work was of a two-fold character —aggressive and conservative. He did not nee the word conservative as opposed to Liberalism, but as opposed to ag- gressiveness. It was aggressive inasmuch as it was in- tended to bring into the fold of Christ those who did not attend any place of worship, and it was conservative in that it had also for its object the building up in the faith those who at present belonged to the church. It was not a time to make complaints and damp the enjoyment of those pre- sent, yet it must be said that the mission was not as successful: as. a true servant of God would wish it to be. But it had done one good thing—it had elicited the services of the laity. Until Borne 15 or 20 years ago, every- one supposed that the parson must do all the work. It was true he ought ever to take the lead in all spiritual matters and undertakings; but it was absurd to suppose he could do everything. In old times it was thought necessary to have a magnificent church and a full-fledged minister before a religious service could be conducted •, and therefore the little villages had to do without a church. A better state of things existed now; the lay members of the church had begun to think it was their duty to supplement the efforts of the minister. They were often told that they were per- petual beggars. That was true, for there was always some- thine.' for which liars cash was required, but it was compara- tively easy to get money. The difficulty lay in personal service, of which there was a great lack. There was always something for everyone to do in the church, and he very earnestly solicited the help of all.—The Rev. T. Manton- Armson proposed a vote thanks to the gentlemen who con- duct the Sunday morning's service in the Mission Room, and also the teachers and office bearers of the Sunday school. He reminded them that it was no disgrace, but rather an honour, to be employed in training the minds of the young people. There were many great statesmen who did not think it beneath their dignity to attend a Sabbath school, and if these men, who had so great a strain on their minds during the week, willingly sacrificed their comfort and ease to the good of others, surely men whose brains were not so heavily taxed might come forward and help in the Work.—Mr. Lello replied on behalf of the teachers.— During the evening several ladies and gentlemen sang songs, of which the following is the programme:—" Song of the brotherhood,/ choir; "Monarch of the woods," Mr. Eidson ; Mr. Imison Hor- ton; " Good bye, sweeti lGarlic," h,"OrnMer, Davies the Saromebody's coming," Mrs. White; "March of the men of "The old woman andsw Jolly Uncle Jack," Miss Morris • pianoforte duet, "Home, not," Miss Horton • "Night r. div.head: CHURCH- EXTENSION AT WIDNES,
div.p: CHURCH- EXTENSION AT WIDNES,
IMPORTANT BAZAAR.

On Weiirlsday, a bazaar, on a scele of such magnitude as is rarely seen in Widnes, was opened in the Volunteer Hall by Mr. Clarke Apinall, J.P., of Liverpool, in connec- tion with the beautiful church of St. Ambrose, Halton View, the foundation stone of which was hid some time ago by Sir R. Assheton Cross, the then Home Secretary. The objects of the bazaar may be succinctly stated in thc words of a circular issued by the friends of the church as follows: —"The want of Church accommodation in Widnes, until recently, was a by-word throughout the district. After many ineffectual attempts to remedy such a sad state of things, in 1374 a few of the raanufacturas of Widnes, and other gentlemen, joined in a scheme for Church extension in Widnes, and proposed to build two churches—one in Farnworth, the other in St. Mary's parish. Three of the large firms, and one gentleman connected with another firm, put down their names for £l,OOO each, another gentlemen for £2OO, and three others for £lOO each, to build a church first in the parish of Farnworth. The scheme, however, for various reasons, was delayed for many years after its con- ception; but, at last, in 1878, there was again a movement made, and a public meeting was called in Widnes, at which the surviving promoters of the scheme agreed to throw their subscriptions into a common fund, for the erection of two churches, and to proceed at once with the building of the church for Farnworth parish. A building committee was elected, who were authorised to build the chancel and part of the nave and aisles of the church for a sum not exceeding £3,000. This was accordingly forthwith commenced, but when the foundation had been laid the parishioners of Farnworth became aware what an un- shapely building it would be, and foresaw, moreover, that the accommodation would be insufficient for the congrega- tion that bad been got together in the meantime in St. Ambrose Mission Room. They therefore resolved to petition the Building Committee to extend the nave and aisles to their full proportions, guaranteeing to provide £l,OOO towards the £1,200 which the additional work was estimated to cost. To this request the Building Committee assented ; . and the Church now stands in all its fair proportions, and the • large congregations every Sunday testify to the wise forethought of the guarantors. The £l,OOO has been nearly I paid off—about £2OO remaining still to be found. Local ' resources have been exhausted in raising the £BOO, and it is hoped that the proceeds of the bazaar will clear away the balance, and also produce a sufficient sum for the endow- • ment and consecration of the Church, so that a district may ' be assigned, and an independent parish established." The attendance at the opening ceremony was large and and influential. Amongst those present were the Revs. G. Holloway, vicar of Farnworth; Allen Spooner, senior curate of Farnworth; J. Holden, curate of the same place; J. Wright-WEliams, vicar of Widnes; J. H. Cummings and J. Tessyman (Wesleyan Methodists), and Messrs. John Brock, J.P., Henry Brummer, James T. Allen, (clerk to the Widnes Local Board), Eustace Carey, H. Kershaw, F. H. Park- hurst, and James Whitley. The Rev. G. Holloway commenced the proceedings by calling upon Mr. Clarke Aspinall to open the bazaar. Mr. Clarke A SPINALL, J.P., who was received with loud applause, said those of them at Liverpool who were con- cerned in the welfare of their Church, spoke very frequently of Widnes and its church necessities, of which they were all very conscious. He hoped that the spirit which appeared to be manifested by that, and he thought, most satisfactory I gathering that day, in the matter of extending their church accommodation, would call forth from neighbours far and wide—and more especially from influential neighbours, real and substantial help in the work in which they were so eagerly and so earnestly engaged, and which was one, he thought, which could only commend itself to the good feel- ing of all parties who knew anything about it. Might be just state that he understood that fine Drill Hall was within the ecclesiastical, or parochial, jurisdiction of their friend Mr. IVright-Williams, and, therefore, they must all feel—as they were in a certain sense—that they were trespassing upon that gentleman's preserves, and that they owed thanks to him for his indulgence in not ordering them to be prose- cuted, as trespassers usually were. (Laughter and applause). He was, however, sure that Mr. Wright-Williams would feel, with them all, that auiongst Christian people—there should be no such thing as trespassing when they stepped over one another's threshold in order to help those who stood in need. The condition of Widnes in church matters was pretty well known to him (the speaker), though much better known to themselves; and they were all aware that Mrr Wright-Williams had a good deal of the burden and heat of the day cast upon him, because his church was more or less responsible—of course only responsible to the extent of the vicar's capacity to do the work, for a man could scarcely be held to do what he was physically unable to accomplish—for the parish. They all knew that the condition of the parsih was one which involved Mr. Wright-Williams iri very great personal arduousness and effort, and in a vast deal of that anxiety which every conscientious clergyman mast feel towards towards the num- ber of persons who were, in a sense, committed to his care, and who in a much more real sense, he was quite unable to care for as he would wish. Well, Widnes, as far as Mr. Wright-Williams was responsible for its spiritual and moral teaching. meant about 16,000 people; but they knew that it was merely a child, though a very large and well grown child, of the old parent at Farnworth. That place by its situation in an agricultural centre had now only about 8,000 persons to be cared for and ministered to, and the church of which they were especially to speak that day—the church of St. Ambrose—relieved Farnworth even of some of its cares and anxieties in regard to the 8,000 Christians who were in that particular parish. The Church of St. Ambrose was very well filled, he was told, especially at its evening service. That could easily be explained, if time permitted', because they knew that working people had difficulties in the way of attending divine worship as some of them would wish in the early part of the day. The need which existed for the church was shown by the way in which its services were frtquented, and he was informed that a large proportion of the congregation—to quote the words as they were spoken to him—was made up of working men. The chto.ellt was at present only a chapel of ease to the mother church at Earn- worth, and it could not be set apart—that was absolutely and permanently—to religious uses, it, at present, being only licensed, like any schoolroom might be, for the purpose of divine worship. It could not be eonsecrated, or if they pre- ferred the term dedicated for ever, so long as it and time should last, to the sacred uses for which it had been built without an endowment fund of some sort being found, or appropriated for the purpose. Mr, Bitoor J.P., who was received with cheers, so that after the admirable address which tney had had from Mr. Aspinall, he was sure they would all join with him in ten- dering to that gentleman a very hearty vote of thanks for coming there to day, at some inconvenience to himself, and al:making to them in the kind and sensible way in which he had.(Applause.) Toe Rev. George HOLLOWAY remarked that he had very great pleasure in seconding the vote to Mr. Aspinall for his most able, interesting and admirable address. ' The resolution was carried with acclamation.

Mr. ASPINALL, in Te:s.c:O-U-ding: observed that it was a great pleasure to him to be thanked he frankly admitted that he appreciated it most sincerely. He knew no body of men whom they ought to think it a privilege to help more than the clergy. They as lay folk—some richer than others, but all of them fairly well to do—sometimes had not had half the education which a clergyman bad had; they had not had half the money spent upon them in their earlier career; but how differently they were paid when the reckon- ing came! the clergy were not only spent, but they spent from day to day on their behalf, as they, all knew. They were always to the five as citizens as wen as ministers, and accepted their oblizationns cheerfully in both capscities ; and be maintained that what they wanted throughout the whole country was that the clergy should be better paid, better supported, and that they should not have people lugubriously groaning about the parochial system breaking down, and such like rubbish. The parochial system would never break down if the laity of England would be as methodical as generous, and as thoughtful in the Spiritual work which it ought to be their privilege to do, as they were in the secular work, which it was greatly to their advantage to do in their own interest:. (Applause.)

. . _ . .. This concluded the opening proceedings, and the practical business of the day commenced. Immediately afterwards a private luncheon was held in the centre of " Ye olde Englysh Markett Playce.” The hall had been fitted up in such a manner as to re- present an English market place in the 16th century. with an ancient market cross in the centre, and, in many respects, the idea had been very well carried out. Above each stall was the full representation of old fashioned gabled houses, with their rude timbers, small panes, many coloured blinds and pointed fronts, with overhanging eaves. The stalls were, however, not given names in old English. There was also no attempt made to emulate the glories of similar bazaars which have been held in some of the large towns of the kingdom, where the "dames and mistresses" have been splendidly attired at great expense. At a bazaar on a similar principle, held recently, we read of Germany being represented by the fair and gentle Marguerite, in a typical dress of black velvet, trimmed with white fur and muslin; the Puritans by a lady in an elegant brown satin dress; Mary Queen of Scots by a fair creature attired in a killed ruby brocade petticoat with panier, a large Marie Stuart ruffle of net, edged with pearls, and from her waist depended a rosary of large pearls and a magnificent crucifix; Mrs. Page and sweet Ann Page, the elderly dame being dressed in a black velvet petticoat, v.S.th Henry the Eighth ruff, scarlet hose, and high heeled boots, and a aogat loaf bat of black velvet; Mrs. Primrose, mentioned in Goldsmith'ti 1 , "Vicar of Wakefield," wearing a petticoat of gold satin, flounced with point lace; a lady of the Queen Anne period with a petticoat of light ruby, a tunic of pompadour, and ruff to match, and grey curled wig; the Duchess of Devonshire, with a puffed and flounced petticoat of old gold figured satin and lace, a tunic of gold brocade, a Brussels lace fichu, secured with arrows of gold, set with pearls aod rubies, and powdered, curled hair; a court lady of the period of Louis the XIV., wearing a Reubens hat with pink feathers and a quilted petticoat of pale pink and pompadour panier. Luckily for our representative, no such costumes had, to be described in connection with the Widnes bazaar, or he would have had to engage the help of some fair mil- liner who was thoroughly well up-in her business in order to do justice to the dresses of the ladies. We understand that at one part of the preliminary arrangements in connec- tion with the bazaar a proposal to dress the ladies in a cos- tume suited to the century intended to be represented was considered, but the decision was come to—and we think very wisely—that it would involve the expenditure of a large sum of money which might be appropriated in the purchase of goods. Each of the ladies who attended the stalls, how- ever, store a mob cap, and most of them sateen aprons. The ladies who presided at the stalls were:— No. I—Mrs. Minton, Misses Newman, Davies (Appleton) and A. Hulme. No. 2—Mrs. Holloway, Miss Fletcher, Miss, Haddock, and Mrs. Henry Cross. No. 3—Mrs. Valentine, Mrs. Speakman, Mrs. Callandar, and Miss Houghton (Crow Wood). No. 4—Misses Cooper, Knight, Carrie Knight, and Hilbert. No. s—Mrs. Burrill, Mrs. Parkes. Mrs. Bullough, and Miss Rainford. No. 6—Mrs. Brumer, Mrs. Booth, Mrs. Wilson, Mrs. J. Knight, and the Misses McClellan, Carrie Deacon, Edith Carey, A, Moule, S. Moule, and Brock. The various stalls were abundantly supplied with articles which included some of every class usually seen at such gather- ings; but it may interest our readers if we notice a few of the principal. At No. 1 were numerous sofa cushions, worked in wool, at prices ranging from 10s. &I. to 255.; a marvellous tea tray made of beaded blue silk, and marked with the interesting figures 42si the flower stands at 40s. the pair, severd interesting oleographs, a splendid scrap album, marked .£4.; a bust of a young gentleman named Mr. Wm. Sadler, who is sturlyint for 3 sculptor, and which displays considerable 4bility ; and a pletty painting of a stag-hound, after Landaeer. by Mr. Charles Davies, of Appleton. The goods on No. 2 stall wlich call for special mention were several handsomely worked satin cushions, satin and velvet worked bracketa. sonv, mignizicent dolls, amongst which was one marked 505., and anoth.,r 425. ; a lovely cushion, price 525. ed.., with an orange satin ground on which were sere. al dihoies ; a nun.b ,r ot Christmas mottoes and decorations, including some by liss Black. borne, of Hale Hall ; some very chaste specimens of Wor- cester china; a point lace apron on satin, valued at 255., and a large number of anti-macassars of all sizes. On No. 3 stall were two gipsy tables, one with velvet top and cruet work, and feet in black and gold; two handsome dolls, one with satin bodice and velvet skirt, trimmed with tarlatan, and marked 30s" and another in pink and white, the price of which was 425.; sofa cushions in great variety; several foot-stools, made of fine beaded rug work (30s. the pair) ; a very pretty cruet stand; a sofa blanket, worked by a . little girl aged seven years, which brought the large sum of 355., a liquor stand at 425., and a great variety of under- clothing. The stall numbered four was well stocked, and amongst the goods was a handsome gipsy table in crewel work, value £4; a representation in cork of St. Ambrose's church, executed by a boy named Master Fred. Allen; a lovely doll's swinging cot, with full dressed baby in pink sateen and lace, price £5; a breakfast stand of chaste design, contributed by Mrs. Holloway, price 42.; a beautiful pen and ink etched table border, at 205.; a bracket made of black satin, ornamented with honeysuckles' and a pretty doll's bed. The goods on stall No. ei embraced a splendidly dressed bride, preserved under a glass shade, and marked 50h.—beautiful enough to satisfy the requirements of any love-sick young gentleman; a three-masted vessel made by a workman employed by Mr. Burrill; a number of useful and sensible articles constructed of old oak from the house of the well known Mr.Rushton, formerly of West Bank ; a very fine edition of the works of the great dreamer, presented by Mr. B. Walker, of Haydock-street, Earlestown. At No. 6 stall there were a couple of splendid drawing-room what- nots, marked .£3 each; handsome table borders at 275. 6d. each; a lovely cushion, with a satin ground ornamented with azaleas, valued at 425.; afternoon tea cloths at from Bs. 6d. to 30s. each, in cruel work; a pretty table, presented by Major Cross, the Chairman of the Local Board: and a magnificent white knitted quilt, at four guineas.—The stalls were fitted up by Mr. Burrill, and they came from the establishment of Messrs. Addison and Sons, 40, Manchester. road, Burnley.

Numerous- attractions of a varied description were also provided, including a conjuring entertainment by Professor Weber; a musical entertainment by Mr. Thorpe's string band of twelve performers; a glee party and a number of handbell ringers, a museum of curiosities, and an exhibition of scientific instruments. The bazaar remained open on Thursday and yesterday (Friday). The receipts from the first day were £270. On Thursday the sale realised the sum of £l4O, but we were unable to obtain the proceeds of yesterday, as up to the time of writing the results had not been handed to the treasurer.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. William Bankes and Mr. Thomas. RENEWAL OF GrNPovvnnat LICENSE—Mr. Thos. Hand- ley, ironmonger, applied for a renewal of his present license to keep a gunpowder store, on Runcorn Hill.—No objection being made, the renewal was granted. Scrrom Boman PuosncrrioNs,—Mr. Thomas Bowyer, School Board officer, gave evidence in the following cases : John Bate, Union-street, not sending his daughter to school. Her attendance for the quarter ending September 30th were 28 present and 77 absent. —Wm. Moores, Pennington's-row, child Thomas, attendances for the quarter 22 times present and 82 times absent; John O'Neil, child James, 23 times present and 88 times absent; Wm. Oakes, Brunswick-street, his child John, who had been present 25 times and absent 86 times; Michael Kenyon Parr's-square, child Bridget, 39 times present and 72 iime's absent; Thomas Laylands. Taylor's-row, child Margaret, 43 times present and absent 63 times; John Antrobus Spring ‘Gardens, child Margaret, 20 times present and 19 times absent; Patrick Dowda, Gran- ville-street, child Michael, 43 times present and absent 69 times; James Cunliff, Cooper-street, child Maria, present 20 times and absent). Michael Calengan, 29, Brunswick- street, child Mary Helen, present 37 times absent 74; John Tomkinson, child Hannah, 7 times present and 103 absent. —Each defendant had ss. including costs to pay. USING PROFANE LANGUAGE.—Annie Jenks and Mary Wilson were charged with using profane language in High- street, on the let inst.—Sergeant Morris proved the case, and the defendant Mary Wilson was fined 10s. and 9s. 6d. costs, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. A warrant was issued for the apprehension of the other defendant, who did not appear.—Louisa Spencer pleaded guilty to a similar charge, and was also fined 10i. and 9s. Ocl. costs, or 14 days.

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT WIIISTON.—On Wed nesday, a fatal accident happened to Richard Swift (45)' collier, whilst following his usual vocation at Carr's Colliery, Whiston. About half-past twelve o'clock at noon, whilst Swift was getting coal,a quantity of the roof fell upon 'him. The accident was witnessed by a " drawer " named Henry Booth, and assistance being at hand deceased was got out of the dibis at once and conveyed home, and Dr. Morris's assistant was called in. Deceased, however, suc- cumbed to his injuries at half-past six o'clock the same evening. ,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Several thousand operatives of the Staffordshire potterieS hare struck work for an advance of wages. At Captoquin Petty Sessions yesterday, a respectable farmer's wife named 3larke, was committed to trial for boy. cotting a land agent: A serioup boiler explosion took place yesterday at the District Iron and Steel Company's Works, Smethwick. Four men were injured, two not being expected to recover. At a meeting of the Thomastown Board of Guardians, yesterday, resolutions were adopted condemning fox hunting in the country. Sever.l incendiary fires have occurred in the district.

M. Ferry and his colleagues in the French Ministry, on Thursday placed their resignation in the hands of President Grevy, and it was accepted. M. Gambetta has been called upon to form a new Cabinet. TIVERTON Nossimaxion.—The objection to the nomina- tion papers of Mr. Loosemore was overruled by the Mayor, and both Viscount Ebrington (Liberal) and 24r. Loosemore (Conservative) will go to the poll on Monday. It is a very costly thing to contest North Lincolnshire. The published accounts of the election show that Mr. Low- ther's expenses were £5,548, and Colonel Tomline's 1,5,383, a total of £10,931 expended in a constituency numbering 10,63 E).

Revolver shots were fired into the house of Mrs. Davies, widow, residing at Cuncea, last night. The children had a narrow escape. In the morning a notice was found on the door warning Mrs. Davies not to deal with certain shop. keepers.

It is announced that the sentence of death passed upon Margaret Messenger, the young girl who last week was con- victed at the Cumberland Assizes of the wilful murder of an infant entrusted to her care, has been respited during Her Majesty's pleasure. Last night Thomas Poole, of Derry Boyle, and Raw Kerney, of Athenry, and a young man named Nebelly, were arrested under the Coercion Act, and lodged in Galway gaol. Four suspects were taken to Clonmel under a strong escort and lodged in gaol.

We regret to announce the death of Richard Bisset Hall.. well from rapid consumption, on the 9th instant. Deceased was a celebrated gentleman cricketer, and in his day acknow. ledged to be the best amateur wicket keeper. Re has of late been engaged on thi press, more especially in the service of the Central Nerve,

Mr Parnell has written from Kilmainham to the leading member of County Wicklow hunt enclosing a cheque as his subscription towards the hounds and stating that he is strongly in favour of maintaining hunting, and hopes that it will not be stopped.

At a largely attended meeting of tenant farmers of Box- burghshire and Berwickshire, held at Kelso yesterday, reso- lutions were carried demanding immediate readjustment of rents and conditions as the only remedy for the present de- pression. A return to Protective Articles was condemned. The first peso before the Land Commissioners in the West of Ireland came on at Ballina on Thursday. It was an- nounced that the landowner, a lady, had come to a compro- mise with the tenant—had in fact agreed to accept £8 10s. per year, instead of £l7 as heretofore—and the "fair rent" was formally settled on this basis for 15 years. The case is regarded as one full of significance. In another case in the same neighbourhood which has been arranged Out of court, it is understood that the reduction is from £6 to £2 10s. The Right Hon. the Speaker visited the Premier daring he sitting of the Cabinet yesterday, and conferred with the Ministers respecting the adoption of new rules for the House of Commons. It is still under discussion and will not be forwarded until farther meetings of the Cabinet have been held, but it was proposed not only to revise the rules of Legislature proceedure so as to check 'obstruction, but to lighten the duties of the House by divesting it to a large extent of the private legislation.

A deputation from the Manchester Chamber of Commerce waited on Lord Hartington urging the removal of the Indian import duties. His lordship, in reply, said it would be extremely inexpedient while the Budget was under consi- deration to announce any positive conclusion that might have been arrived at. The pledges he had given were con- fined to the abolition of the duties on grey goods, but an alteration should be made as soon as the financial condition of India permitted. His lordship, in conclusion, pointed out the danger of reliance on the opium revenue, which was occupying much attention.

GOLBORNF. GoLBoRNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—OR Monday evening a goodly number of members met in the large room of the Association, when Mr. Charles Hall read a paper on the County Franchise. For the purpose of raising a discussion, Mr. Hall took the negative and argued from a Conservative point of view. He tried to show that the ex- tension ot the franchise, taking a continental view of things, would not be beneficial to this country, too much power would be given to the lower classes which would effect the aristocracy of this country and might cause a revolution. However, the majority were of opinion that, if the working classes in the boroughs were qualified to vote, it was only just that those who crossed the boundry line should have a vote also. For this reason, that the working classes in the counties were as intelligent as those within the boroughs. Comparisons were made as to the intelligence displayed by some of the voters at Wigan at the last election there. Mr. Hall received a warm reception, and he admitted that it was only right that as the working classes in the boroughs were allowed to vote he could not but admit that they ought to have the same privilege granted in the county. Yet look- ing back to ancient history he was afraid the people might fall into the same errors, and this might cause a reaction tvhich might bring about the same results as in days gone by—which meant nothing more or less than a revolution. It was, however, unanimously voted that there ought to be the same privileges granted to the counties as in the boroughs, and that the present Government ought to deal with it.

HOLT Tunrrry SCHOOLS, RIISOORN.—These schools have now been enlarged, so as to provide accommodation for 80 additional children. Tax PHEuroH Mus.can.—On Monday, John/L.3plusll Simpson, 21, clerk, was tried for the wilful mttider of his sweetheart, Ann Ratcliffe, a girl of 16, daughterof a Preston innkeeper, on the morning of the 3rd of August last. The prisoner had deluded the girl, with promises of marriage, and on the morning of her death she left home to meet him for the purpose, as she believed, of being married. They called at a public house in North-road, Preston, where they were served with lemonade and a few minutes after that beverage had been supplied to them the landlady's daughter was horrified to see the deceased running towards the door with a dreadful wound in her throat, from which blood was streaming. The deceased then turned back into the room, and fell dead upon the floor. Simpson was found sitting in the room, and when he was asked who had cat the girl's throat, he said "It is me." For the defence, the theory was Set up that the wound was self-inflicted, but there was no evidence that the deceased had had any weapon in her possession, whereas it was found that the razor with which the wound was caused corresponded 'exactly with one which was missing from a hairdresser's shop where the prisoner had called three or four days previously. The jury found the prisoner guilty tf wilful murder, and when he was asked if he had anything to say why sentence of death should nut be pronounced upon him, he replied, "No, sir, I'm perfectly satisfied." Mr. Justice •Kay then sentenced the prisoner to be hanged, remarking that the deceased had been most bar- barously murdered, and that he fully agreed in the verdict of the jury. The prisoner left the dock as he had entered it, with a light step and utterly unmoved.

THARSIS SULPHUR AND COPPER COMPANY'S MEETING. —An extraordinary meeting of the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Company was held on Wednesday, in Glasgow, Mr. Charles Tennant presiding, for the purpose of considering special resolutions,Vroviding, first, that the company may from time to time, by special resolution, modify the con- ditions contained in the memorandum of the association so as to reduce its capital to such an extent and in such man- ner as may be determined; and secondly, to modify the conditions contained in the memorandum of the association, and sub-divide its shares into shares of similar amount as fixed by the memorandum of the association.—The Chair- man, in moving the first resolution, said :—Assuming that we place the shares at £4O per share, we shall get a sum of £360,000, of which £113,310 will go to the cle4tor and capital account, and the remainder, reprbsenting the pre- mium, £246,720, to the debtor and reserve account. The cash in bank will thus be increased by this total of £300,000, which we shall devote to the paying off of our debentures as they fall due, the amount of which is now 5,355,600. The reserve fund will thus stand at £318,844, making, with our railway sinking fund of £lOO,OOO, a total of £416,844, Our next proposal is to give the option to shareholders of having their shares converted into "share warrants to bearer." This privilege will in all probability be largely availed of by our French Mende, who already bold about one-third of our stock. By the send resolution which I shall have to submit to you, the board asks you to place in the hands of the company the necessary powers should the shareholders at any time decide in favour of a sub-divison of the stock. There is still another change in our arrangements which I must bring before you, and which you will, I am sure, approve, viz., to balance or books at the end of the year instead of the 28th of February. Our annual meeting will be held in April, and our dividend paid in one sum in May as formerly. Bv these imput.ort changes the position of the company will be simpliaedt and strengthened, and the board, therefore, recommends for your approval and adoption—The motion ra ,pros 5180 poed the the chairman was carried tinn MOW motion with reference to the Sub-division of stock.
