div.head: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN.
[SPEciAL.]___ No. XXIV. NAZARETH TO CARMEL (CoynNuED).

- --- Te return to Sepphoris and the Arab school, one of the I boys, at the request of his teacher, read a portion from the Koran. Sitting down with the book upon his knee, he swayed his body backwards and forwards as he intoned with great distinctness every word, resting on the last syllable of each sentence, and giving it a long-drawn utterance. We thought if our English children could only be taught to read the scriptures with half the care that these children read the Koran, what a.happy thing it would be for England, and yet, in deference to our accursed denominationalism, the ' Book of Gad must be banished from our national schools by Act of Parliament. The guide book informs us that Sep- phoris was a very important town at the commencement of the Christian era; that, having been rebuilt by Herod Antipas, it became the largest and strong st place in Galilee. Strange, therefore, that no mention is made of it in the New Testament. Would the fact of its being a fortified town account for it? or the fact of its being in the course of passing out of the condition of a conquered and demolished town into that of a more warlike stronghold than ever. Some people sav that Christ never spent one night in a walled or fortified city, but kept to the open country, or to open towns and villages. His retirement to Bethany every night during his stay in Jerusalem lends countenance to the idea.

CANA. Cana of Galilee was our destination after leaving Sep- phoris. Instead of looking for it at Kana el Jelil, two or three miles north of Sepphoris, a village now admitted by all careful explorers of ancient sites to be the veritable Cana of the New Testament, we went forward to Kefr Kenna (an hour and a quarter's ride), and encamped there. This village disputes with Kena el Jelil the honour of the marriage feast, and the Greek church ma,es capital out of a jar which, they say, is one of the water-pots in which the Water was turned into wine. As we entered the village, it had a very Oriental aspect. Around the large well were gathered a number of cattle, which the herdsmen were supplying with water by lifting large flat vessels to the Stone fencing, out of which three oxen drank at a time. The women also stood in the water, filling their skins and chat- tering as Arab women only can. We were more annoyed with the intrusion of the villagers upon our tent-ground than we had been before. With less than his usual care our dragoman, had pitched our tents on ground which had been recently ccupied by beasts of other travellers. The stench was intolerable, and the inroad of fleas--Saracenic! The fleas themselves, real Turks! blood-thirsty barbarians! I have no pleasant recollection of Kefr Kenna, and, being assured of its counterfeit character as Cana of Galilee, I took no pains to make myself acquainted with its peculiari- ties, but rejoiced when the morning came, and we were fairly on our way to to the Sea of Tiberias.

SEA OF GALILEE. Not far from Kefr Kenna we passed the road that leads down the hill side at the back of Nazareth and joins the one along which we were travelling. Adown that mountain path to the right, and along this very way, the holy feet of Jesus must have trod, His heart wrung with sorrow, after His first rejection by His people. Nor have we any proof that He ever retraced His steps to His native town. Our road for some miles lay through a long and fruitful valley; and, in the afternoon, we passed Hattim, the great battle- fields of the Crusaders, and the traditional Mount of Beautitudes. Then we began to descend the wide and steep ravine that leads down to the shores of Genneaareth. Our first view of the lake was from an elevation of 700 fact. Its northern margin breaks first on the vision, then gradually opens Out as you descend and wind round the hill that overlooks Tiberias. The mountain ranges, stretching from the shores of the lake far to the north, and bounded by the glorieus Hermon, {ere beyond alladcriptiOn beautiful. The lake itself lay glistening i.e. the sunlight, yet I could scarce persuade myself that the sea of Galilee wasbefore me, so small and insignificant it looked to have been the scene of so many mighty, such unparalleled events. The idea of a storm in such a basin of water seemed I inconceivable. But, in respect to its size, its area hourly grows upon you, as the lightness and purity of the atmosphere give place to the shadows, clouds, and darkness that oftimes rest upon it. Then, as to its susceptibility to storms we had a very striking indication of this characteristic soon after we arrived, and a most alarming experience of it before we left its shares. Our tents were pitched close to the lake, just above Tiberias, arid, in the calm of the evening I was standing on its pebbly beach, when, without the slightest breath of wind on the cheek, the waves began to roll in, and the surface of the water to look troubled. The only possible solution was that a sudden breeze had come down on the opposite side of the lake, and after spending I itself on its surface sent over this commotion as the result. And, we thought, if a slight, and to us imperceptible, breeze, could produce such and effect, no wonder the lake should be lashed into fury and foam when the wilder winds rush down the mountain sides and sweep across its breast. And was it indeed true that we stood by the lake whose waters, in their fiercest moods, had borne the feet of the Son of God, and had once been hushed by him into silence and repose? Was it not here, at Tiberias, that Peter girt his fisher's coat about him and cast himself into the sea? Might it not be on this very shore on which we stand, with its clean white pebbles and myriads of spiral shells, that Jesus lit the fire and pre- pared the fish and bread for His poor toil-worn disciples? What crowded memories flow in upon the mind when the sea of Galilee is mentioned; and now to stand upon its brink, while its wondrous history rolls in upon the memory and stirs every emotion of the soul, should it not awaken and inspire feelings of profoundest gratitude. That I was the subject of such feelings as I stood by the lake, I find my note-book bears witness. It says: "As the scenes which make its history so full of interest rush over the mind in rapid succession. I thank my God with fervent spirit that I have been permitted to behold a spot so sacred, so rich in Divine Memories." And I ant sure I was not alone in these praises and asphatiens. TIBERI AS, Although our tents were pitched no near to Tiberias, I did not venture within its gates. Some of or friends, just before sundown, and before the gates were closed, entered within its ramparts, but they give such a dismal account of its dirty streets, its earthquake-shattered walls, and miserable inhabitants, that I found it an easy matter to persuade myself that, although I had come 3,000 miles to see the Holy Land, I could see all I wanted of the Holy Land without entering Tiberias. The probability is that the present town is not the Tiberias of the Saviour's time. The ruins of an ancient city far more likely to be it, are still visible about a mile to.the south. There we find the remains of thick walls running into the ldke, with broken columns and numerous heaps of black basalt, of which the houses and ramparts must have been built. Next morning, before breakfast, while the ladies were bathing in an improvised tent, whose stakes were driven into the bed of the lake a few feet from the shore, and while the gentlemen had gone far away up the lake for the same purpose, I wandered amid the ruins of the ancient city, and felt deeply interested in tracing the direc- tion of the old walls of an aqueduct, as they ran up toward the hill, and in observing the nature of the fragments. Some of the columns were of beautifully white limestone, and others of light grey granite, both of which must have contrasted very finely with the prevailing basalt, which was black as ebony.. Beyond the ruins to the south are the celebrated hot springs or baths. I looked in and, saw a few patients bathing in a common basin, used alike by men and women. Outside runs a small stream from the base of the hill into the lake. You can scarcely bear your hand in it at forty or fifty yards from its source. The water is almost bitter' in its saltness, and, as there are other similar springs running into the lake, they must give to it more or less of a saline character, which, although not appreciable to the taste in a lake whose waters flow out as rapidly 39 they flow in, may it not be that the Dead Sea, where the water finds no outlet except by evaporation, derives something of its dense and acrid saltness from the long accumulating deposits from the Tiberian spring ? THE SEA OF GALILEE.

In stepping out on the shore after breakfast we found that two boats had been rowed in for our use, to take us to the head of the lake.. Leaving our horses and baggage to go by land to Khan Minjeh—the ancient Bethsaida--Nve embarked in the somewhat rickety boats, each in charge of four Arabs, bound for Tell Hum, or, as lam satisfied to believe, the site of old Capernaum. There would be from twelve to fourteen persons in each boat. We called under the sea-wall of Tiberias, and took in a long net, in doing which we seemed so much in character with the place that we bore with patience the delay. As we sailed up the lake its surface was as smooth as glass and the sun poured down upon us its scorching rays. Our Arab boatmen did not spare themselves, but pulled at their oars with wonderful spirit and energy. It took us two hours be reach Tell Hum, and the time being filled up by the aiinging of many familar hymns. I think it must have been to create a diversion that our dragoman perpetrated a most wanton piece of mischief. He and Aboo were sitting at the prow of the boat seeming to enjoy all that was going on, when he slyly filled a small can with 'Water out of the lake, and poured the contents down Aboo's back. The poor fellow cringed and shewed his big white teeth with such a ludicrous grin that we laughed. Aboo tried to pay his master back in his own coin, but only succeeded in bringing upon himself a second sousing. It was no laughing matter for Aboo; he was siezed with a vio- lent cold, and for several days went -about y ,t'l his head hanging down like a bulrush. We gave him a :e aperient medicine, and then he complained to the drav) )11 that we had made him very ill. He coughed and had.) )ain in his chest. The dragoman said it was a bad job. V ten he was reminded of the water he had poured down Abou's back, he very naively replied, "The pain is not in his back, it is in his chest !" One of the friends gave AbGo a little brandy which secured him a good night's rest, and seemed to bring about a reaction. Then his gratitude was so exhuberant that it became more impleasant than his former dark looks. (To be continued next week.)

Sir,—ln your impression of the sth inst. James Kilduff is reported, in speaking at a meeting of ironworkers, that he was not getting sufficient wage to Ceep him and his family. As Kilduff is working at Dallam Forge and one of our puddlers, I have inquired into the amount he has been getting for the 12 weeks ending October 22, 1881, and the following is the result :—Total amount received from office, , £35 16s. 10d., for 62 shifts. Having to pay his underhand half a shift per week for fettling or lighting-up the furnace, that would be 68 shifts at 3s. 6d.—£ll 18s., leaving for himself £23 18s. 10d., or £1 19s. 10d. per week, whilst he lost four shifts. If he had worked the other four shifts, making 66 in the three months, he would have received for himself £25 9s. Bd., or £2 2s. sd. per week. After giving judge as above facts and figures,l shall leave the public to as to the truth of Kilduff's statement. Hoping in future our men will confine themselves to the truth, I am yours, Sic., B. BUDGE, Dallam Forge. P.S.—I think it is also due from me to state that the men on strike would make as much as the above, if not more. November 11, 1881. B. It.

Sir,—We decline to take notice of anonymous communi- catiow, and having stated the facts respecting the dispute with a portion of our puddlers we shall leave the matter to take its course. Before the puddlers left their work we proposed that the question in dispute should be decided by arbitration; this offer the men declined. There is in con- nection with the iron trade a board of arbitration, in South Staffordshire, called "The Wages Board," of which we are members; the objects and constitution of that Board are set out in its rules; the third of which is as follows:—" The Board shall consist of a president, twelve employer repre- sentatives, twelve operative representatives, a chairman (who shall be appointed by the employers' section from among their body), a vice-chairman (who shall be appointed by the operative section from among their body), a secretary appointed by the employers, a secretary appointed by the operatives, and a treasurer appointed by the Board." Rule second, so far as it relates to this subject, is as follows:—"In case of any difference arising at any works, it is intended that it shall be settled by the works representatives, but in case of their failing, it is open to them to refer it to the chairman, vice-chairman, and the two secretaries, who may call the Board together to decide it, if they see fit." We have been ready and willing from the first to refer the case to this Wages Board, and we should have thought that if any man wished to do what was right, here was the means and opportunity of doing it. aVe have communicated with the two secretaries of the Board so far as to let them know that a difference existed, and we think we are not wrong in saying that in their opinion we have done all that the Wages Board requires, and that whoever refuses to accept arbitration in a matter of this kind, proves himself to have a bad case. We will not be drawn into any controversy; these facts are not to be disputed; we have offered a solution of the difficulty, but we do not intend to leave it open for an indefinite time—Yours, dzc. 1 THE PEARSON S.: KNOWLES COAL & IRON COMPANY, LIMITED,

Sir,— Having a great personal inierest in all that occurs respecting this unfortunate difference between Bewsey puddlers and their employers, and wishing to place a few things before the public, with which I think they are unacquainted, in explanation of the course we are pursuing, I shall be glad if you will find room for this in your next issue. Mr. Morris bases his claim to this 3d. reduction upon two things: lot, what Messrs. Monks pay ther pud- dlers; 2nd, country custom. With regard to the first, I hold that the plea that Messrs. Monks pay less per ton for puddling has no more to do with Bewsey than the fact that Monks' men earn more money for the same weight of iron produced, together with an extra, which Bewsey men (1.0 not get, has to do with them. Let us have a fair comparison; and if you say Messrs. Monks pay 7s. 9d. per ton, say,. at the same tine, they pay also 6d, to their men for making that which Bewsey men get nothing for making. So that, although Monks' men are paid less per ton, and perform the same amount of labour, in the end, they earn more Money than the overpaid Bewvy men. I have always been told that Bewsey was the leading works in Lancashire. If so, how is it Messrs. Monks did not follow the leader ? I understand they plead local circumstances, which makes 7s. 9d. at their works equal to Ss. at Bewsey; and the men acknowledge the same thing. Mr. Morris should accept the plea, because he, I believe, was the first to adopt the prin- ciple when dealing with the Dallam men at Wigan, and paying them 7s. 3d. for billets and small bars, instead of the 7s. 9d. Monks' pay or the Sc. paid at Bewsey. Now, sir, as to country custom. I would like to ask Mr. Morris where he goes for it. Let me ask him if it is, or, rather, was, the trade custum to pay 6d. per ton or ld, per heat for making billets. If so, who broke the custom at Dallam, Wigan, a works under his own management? It was the custom to pay in Lancashire 6d. per ton mo,e than was paid in Staf- fordshire. Mr. Morris *its the first to break that custom. It was a trade custom to pay extra for puddling best iron. Mr. Morris pays nothing extra. Let me ask Mr. Morris if it was not the trade custom to pay extra for puddling wire iron. Did he break that custom? I only ask because before he came to Bewsey we worked five heats of wire iron for a day's labour. Now we have to work six and earn less money. Maybe lie can tell us how long it has been the custom to class fettling as half mine and half cinder. Has it not been the custom rather to pay 6d. when meh have used cinder, whether it has been half cinder or all cinder, until he broke the custom some time ago, when the men allowed him to take 3d. off, along with the alteration of fettling? I begin to fear my letter will be too long, so I will give a list of alterations at Bewsey since Mr. Morris has been here? Ist, 6d. per ton off scrap; then 6d. per ton off all round; then altered the mode of working, so that we make one-fifth more iron for the same money; next 3d. per ton for altering fettling, next proposes a scheme instead of the Employers' Liability Act, which was to be all men could desire, but is so moulded that I shall be sur- prised if any sensible man agrees .to it. When, after this, he collies again wanting another 3d., I think the public will agree with us its time to cry hold on, enough. I don't thin, so far as the above shows, Mr. Morris has shown much reverenze for custom. But now he stands amazed, astounded, that men should want to break a custom. But we don't want to break any custom; we claim the 3d. because of the quality of iron we work and local circum- stances, making our labour well worth the money. Mr. Morris talks about arbitration; but he must be a new con- vert, for always up to now he would have no third parties, being able himself to come to terms with his men. The news that our firm give pecuniary support to an arbitration board is rather a surprise to us, as if they have done so for any length of time, they have done so secretly, and to suit their own purpose. But let them pay on, the men are not to be drawn into supporting a board so far away, the members of which know nothing of any peculiar circumstances under which we labour, and we refuse now to be guided by a board in the election of whose officers and the framing of whose rules we have had nothing to do. Mr. Capper is going to send men front the South, is he? Let him find them first. Let me ask him a question. When the employers have refused arbitration, has the employers' secretary defended the men and condemned the masters on the employers' or workmen's evidence alone, and assisted the workmen in defeating the masters? Did the board of which Mr. Capper is oue of the secretaries or did the mastep' secretary, in the Firmstone and puddlers' dispute, advise the employers to black-leg Mr. Firmstone and support the men? We have not asked Mr. Capper to interfere, neither are we members of his board or recognise its authority, and it would be mach more to his credit did he wait until we asked him to advise and represent us. Probably, he forgets the strong terms in which be condemned the action of the employers as a body when here last to receive payment from those he now condemns upon an ex parte statement. What has brought the change? Why is Mr. Capper so ready to assist the class he so lately condemned ? Does lie know we have seen too much of him ever again to coins to hisassistance? Perhaps he will explain how it is he his doing his best to injure the class which has placed him in his present position.—Apoloaisino• for the length of this letter, I remain, PADDLE.

Sir,—The eßclosed advice from St. Paul to Timothy, was sent to me by a rev. gentleman who used, to be the minister at St. John's Chapel, in Warrington. I think your readers as well as myself should have the benefit of this advice. I don't see that it applies particularly to me. Yours, faith- fully, JOHN CROSFIELD Walton Lea, November 11th.

WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. Sir,—As the report of a case which came on for hearing on Friday, the 4th inst., in which I was the appellant, may lead some persons to assume I made a statement with i reference to the quality of the land assessed which s in- correct, I shall be glad with your permission to correct it. One of the committee who professed to know the land intimately said that I stated the land in question was bad land, and he knew it to he some of the bast land in Penketb. The chairman, quoting the words of this guardian, spoke of it as" bad land." This statement I wish to correct. 1 never considered it or thought it bad land, but rather the contrary. What I did say (and to prove this I may refer to the reporters' notes) was that the land, since the brewery had been closed, had remained uncultivated and neglected, and that one half of it was badly drained, or the drains had got

DISGRACEFUL OUTRAGES. Sir,—We would desire to caution the public passing through Widnes after night-fall, more particularly between the railway stations and the Mersey Bridge, as to the dis- gusting conduct of the "Corner Pests who have taken to throwing on passers gutter filth, paint, acid, d:c. We know of several cases in which valuable dresses have been nearly ruined. What are the reasons for such miserable work? Is it envy or pure malice? The police are aware of these outrages, but Ippear unable to detect any in the act. We expect when the perpetrators are caught a very prompt punishment will be dealt out on the spot, and a stop put to conduct that disgraces the town of Widnes.—Yours, Widnes, 10th November, 1881. YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. Dear Mr. Editor,—' have the pleasure of perusing your valuable paper from week to week, and note with pleasure the many changes and reforms which are likely to benefit the inhabitants of your good town. In your issue of the 29th ultimo, I observe the political mania which took hold ot the more matured politicians, the result of which was the formation of a mock parliament, and which is now dis- solved into thin air,—the Speaker's dinner evidently being the most prominent feature of the session,—and in its disso- lution it would seem that a double portion of the political spirit has fallen upon the youth of the community, who, on the parent association's decease, immediately begin to ape politics. I have no doubt it is for the interests of the in- habitants that they should become political sucklings rather than hangers on at the street corners, &c. But there is no reason why either course should be adopted when there is a more excellent way of improving each shining hour ; and to show how this may be accomplished, it is only necessary for me to point to almost every little village in England, Ireland, and Scotland who can boast of a "Young Men's Christian Association," to which is invariably added a literary association, from which much useful information may be had on almost every conceivable subject, by the exchange of the individual opinion of its members. To say nothing of the Christian element, the advantages to be derived are far beyond anything which a political association could hold out, while on the other hand the Christian spirit of such an association tends to check the heated ferments of youthful blood, and prevents the creation of an individuality of feeling which is too often associated with political discussions, if once the young men could see by comparing the position of St. Helens with that of other towns of much less importance, that they are really behind the times. I am sure those of them who have any regard for their religious convictions, and the moral tone of the community generally, they would at once see to the formation of a Young Men's Christian Association being established in their midst, and under the guidance of a few Christian spirited gentlemen the associa- tion would old fair to becoming a permanent institution, and likely to outlive the so-called " Parliamentary Debating Societies." The spirit in which the work of a successful Young Men's Christian Association is carried on is not that of the "miser," who grudges the approach of his neighbour to his own happiness. There is not an association in any town of importance, but has its usual winter course of lectures by which the public may be benefited, and when we come to consider that a public course of lectures in St. Helens is a rarity, at least so far as the newspapers indicate, I think it is not too much to say that if the young men take the matter up they may calculate upon the public sympathy in a cause which has been hailed with satisfaction through- out the length and breadth of the land, and they have already received the assurance of Mr. Hales, the secretary at Liver- pool, that he will do all he can to aid them in their efforts, and I trust that at the next conference of Young Men's Christian Association delegates a favourable report will be ' made by a St. Helens representative. Apologizing for tree- ' passin on your valuable space.—Yours, J. R. B. London, 3rd Nov., 1881.

RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. At the weekly meeting on Tuesday, the proceedings began by the Member for Preston commencing the adjourned debate on the Queen's Speech. He was very much struck with the hopefulness of the document. Speaking of the 3rd clause, he said they had not noticed that progress in trade and commerce which they were led to expect from the speeches of the honourable gentlemen on the other side at the commencement of their present administration. With regard to Ireland, he blamed. the present Government very much for the slack and dilatory way in which they had dealt with that country. He contendel that if they had put on a bold front they would have heard nothing of the blood- shed, outrages mutilations, &c. which had unfortunately been committed. ' The mischief lay at their doer. Com- menting upon the speech made by the Member for Oxford, he contradicted the assertion that Conservatives had opposed the Land Bill tooth and nail, on the other hand they had received from the Conservatives that assent which their consciences had justified them in giving.—The Postmaster- General, in an eloquent speech, urged the folly of listening to the cries which the Conservative party were so apt to resort to ; the false cries which they had heard about ruining the country, especially at the time of the repeal of the Navigation Laws, the repeal of the Paper Duty, the Disestablishment of the Irish Church, and, lastly, on the passing of the Irish Land Act. He believed that the latter would prove a great boon to the country, and it was the duty of every true Liberal to boldly push forward their principles so as to strengthen and consolidate the great and mighty empire in which they lived, and of which they felt so proud.—The Member for Hastings said if he replied to the fallacy of all the arguments of the previous speaker it would take him until that time the following night. (Great laughter, and cries of "Oh, oh !") It was not on account of the difficulty of proving the fallacy of the arguments, but simply because they were so numerous. He dwelt at considerable length upon the present state of Ireland, the country in which judges had said that trial by jury was a farce, where murders had been committed with impunity, houses burned, homes destroyed, and animals tortured and mutilated. He argued that this state of things had been fiomre nto f Swansea, t hi theLa nddeßba i ltle.— was allowed to exist simply because the Prime Minister was the motiondesirous of tryingof th e the Membere experiment I adjourned.—The Member for Birkenhead gave notice that he would ask the Foreign Secretary if the Government had entered into negotiations with Spain for the transfer of "Gibraltar.—The Secretary for Foreign Affairs immediately ' jumped up and began to make a long statement, when he was.interrupted by the Member for Birk.enhead, who thought he was not sticking to the point involved in the question, and appealed to the chair.—After the Speaker's ruling the hon. gentleman stated that no hint bad been thrown out by the Spanish Government on that matter, and the subject,was entirely a myth on the part of the Conservatives.—The Leader of the Opposition gavemotice that he would ask the Premier whether it is the intention of the Government to keep Messrs. Parnell and Dillon in Kilmainham until the expiration of the Coercion Act.—The House then rose.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

ELECTION OF 1.4AY0R., The first meeting of the newly-constitu ed Council was held at the Town Hail, at noon, on Tuesday. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair; Aldermen Davies, Holmes, Kean, Burgess, Chandley, Webster, Thewlis, Harrison, Councillors Monks, Platt Caldwell, Wallington, Dixon, Greening, Brown, Mackie, Pierpoint, Barker, Ridgway, Milner, Woolfall, Sutton, Jeans, Ashton, Litton, Francomb, Whittle, Fairclough, Bprgess, and Crosfield, and Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (treasurer), T Longdin (surveyor), J. H. Gornall (medical officer). That portion of the Council chamber set apart for the public was crowded with ratepayers some time before the proceedings commenced. At the call of His Worship, , The Towle CLERK read the return of members elected at the last election of councillors, which has already appeared in The Examiner. The Maxon then said that his year of office having expired, the next business was the election of mayor for the ensuing year, and he should be glad to hear the remarks of any gentleman. • Alderman BOWLES begged to propose the following resolu- tion: "That John Richard Pickmere' Esquire, one of the aldermen of this borough.- be re-elected mayor for the ensuing year, until the acceptance of office by his succesor." He said the course which the Council was about to pursue reminded him somewhat of a tale he heard of a min who was dismissing a servant. The servant would not go, and said, "If you don't know when you have got a good servant I know when Dave (iota good master." He thought the Council was thoroughly alive to the fact that the Mayor, during the two years which had just expired, and during the year in which he held office some time ago, had fulfilled the onerous duties of the office he had so worthily held, in a manner which had given great satisfaction to the Corpora- tion, and also to the inhabitants of the town at large. (Hear, hear.) In discharging the duties which bad fallen upon him as chief magistrate of the borough, he thought the decisions the Mayor had given and the manner in which he had upheld the dignity of that court reflected great credit upon him; as well as the manner in which he had invariably presided over the Council. The thorough impartiality which he had exercised, and the respect he had gained by that course itidnced the Council with great satisfaction to ask him to accept the office of Mayor of Warrington for the third year. (Hear, hear) He did not know that be need say anything more upon the subject for anything be might say was fully known by all the members of the Council and the inhabitants of the town, and he therefore concluded by simply moving the resolu- tion. (Applause.) Alderman CRANDLEY, in seconding the resolution, said he would not add to what Alderman holmes had said as to the way the Mayor had discharged his municipal duties;social, and other duties. His career had been of credit to himself, and satisfaction to those by whom he was surrounded. It was a circumstance perhaps unique in the annals of the Council that His Worship should be called to fill the office of Mayor for the fourth year. It must be gratifying to his feelings to know he had merited the distinction. At the same time they, as a Council, must be fully alive to the great responsibility Alderman Pickmere had undertaken, and they felt universally by accepting that responsibility he had only added another obligation to those already incurred on behalf of the Council. (Applause.) They did feel that obligation, and they considered that in undertaking the office for the fourth time, he had conferred a favour on the Corporation and on the ratepayers at large. They were all quite aware that the Mayor in the first instance, with very becoming dignity, declined, from the best of motives, to serve for another year. He was earnestly solicited by his friends to accept office another year, and he consented, but not without very great reluctanea on his part. It was at the lamest solicitation of his friends he consented to allow himself to be again nominated. His worship had had placed before him a regulation from the members of the Council—from the whole of the mem- bers present—(no, no)—at the meeting. A second was called for the purpose of enabling any one else to have an opportu- nity of confirming the resolution which was passed. (Hear, hear). They found, whatever might be said to the contrary, that there was not a single dissentient amongst those who had already signed the requisition. Some very proper re- marks were made as to the desirability or necessity of call- ing a second meeting. Were the Council a body of men accustomed to change their purpose, and was it necessary another meeting should be called? That was a very proper enquiry. But they had no doubt that the same unanimity would prevail as at the first meeting; that unanimity did prevail; and they unanimously came to the conclusion that none could serve them so well as Alderman Pickmere. He need only say the Mayor would have the heartfelt co-opera- tion of the Council during his next year of office; and was sure be would be elected. (Applause). He would have an opportunity of adding fresh laurel leaves to those he had already won, and of which he might be justly proud. (Ap- plause). Alderman KEAN added his testimony to the great satis- faction Alderman Pickmere had given during his term of office; and that was, he believed, the sole reason the Coun- cil were anxious he should undertake the office again. They all felt certain they would have the same result in the future as in the past. He knew it was a great undertaking to ac- cept the office so often; but if the Mayor was willing to serve, the Council were williogto give him all the support they could. (Applause.) They were sure they would meet with nothing but Success; and that there would be no die- appointment wliatever. He therefore hoped his worship would accept the offide once more. (Applause). • Alderman BATIES said it was his duty to read first the resolution passed at the second meeting of the members of the Council asking his worship to become Mayor of Warring- ton for another year. Thera seemed to be some little mis- giving perhaps in Alderman Pickmere's own mind, as to the unanimous, and necessity—the this being very properly so ; and there was an opportunity given the previous night to see whether the Council was still unani- mons in the selection of that gentleman as Mayor. He might tell him that at a very numerous meeting in the mem- bers of the Town Council, held on Tuesday night n that room, the resolution was not only unanimous, but he thought Alderman Pickntere would have been very pleased indeed if he had heard the words of sympathy that were naturally called for on Tuesday morning for him—(bear, hear, and applause)—and for the very great esteem spoken to by every member of the Council Pat happened to be present. There were nearly all the members present; and he was pleased to think he was the vehicle to-day to convey to his worship the expressions of regard and esteem, and of the anxious hope—stronger words were used than the resolution conveys—and wish and desire, in the interests of the Council and in the interests of the town, that be should allow himself to stand for office another year. lie would read the resolution passed: " Resolved, that the re- quisition to the Mayor to accept office on the 9th day of November instant, which he acceded to at the last meeting, be confirmed " ; and that confirmation was given with cheers and words of sincere regard for his worship. He had another pleasing duty to perform because whatever the Council might do in that room they did from their conviction that I their judgment was right. No influences were brought to bear in discussing whether it was desirable the Council I should make Alderman Pickmere Mayor; but every man spoke from his own point of judgment, and they came to that unanimous vote. After that 'vete had been come to he read to the members of the Connell, that it was not confined to the Council, but that it was the unanimous wish of the inhabitants of the town that he shonld be again elected. (Applause.) He was sorry there was occasion to refer to something that did take place on Tuesday morning; but it would be pleasing to know that the inhabitants of the town could not rest satisfied until they kid expressed their deep sympathy and regard, and had conveyed to his worship what they felt. It came, he knew, from circumstances which had come to Ms knowledge spontaneously from the ratepayers out- side. Not a single member of the Council knew that this was being done. It reads as follows :-1--We the undersigned rate- payers of the Borough of Warrington, deshe to express our very strong disapproval, of the anonymous and unmanly attack which has been made upon you. (Applause.) We do nor envy the feelings of the individual who could write and circulate such a production. We abstain from all com- ment upon the proceedings of the Corporation, as being, under the circumstances, uncalled for; but we cannot re- frain from expressing to you our sense of the obligation we feel for the admirable manner in which, at the request of your fellow towesmen, you have for the last two years dis- charged the responsible duties of Mayor. Bth November, 1881. (Applause.) Having read the signatures, the Alderman proceeded to say he was pleased to read every man's name; for if he were a ratepayer of Warrington to-day he would be proud to have his name read over to express sympathy and regard for his worship. He could only say that Mr. Beamont was not well enough to come to town; but Mr. Robert Davies assured him he-would be very sorry indeed if he had not an opportunity of joining the inhabitants and ratepayers of Warrington in showing how deeply they regarded Alderman Pickmere; and they might rest perfectly satisfied that the fact of making him Mayor again VMS expressing the voice of the town. (Ap- plause.) He had taken some trouble to enquire throughout the town whether there was anyone who` had the slightest objection to the course the Council were taking; but he had. not met with a single individual who had not expressed his entire satisfaction with the course they were pursuing. Alderman BURGESS could not allow himself to give a silent vote on this occasion. He could not allow the opportunity to pass without saying how thoroughly he endorsed, and entirely be agreed with every word that had been said by the preceding speakers with reference to the appointment of Mayor that day; and perhaps he might do so with more confidence than be otherwise should from the fact that he believed at this moment all the gentlemen composing the Town Council of Warrington—he happened to be one who was first elected to that body, and this was the first time it had come under his notice that a gentleman should be pro- posed for election for the high office of Mayor for the fourth time—felt that if there was anything Alderman Pickmere need to be proud of in his career in passing through life, it was the fact that his fellow-townsmen in Council assembled thought his conduct was such during the three years he had gone through, that it entitled him lobe again asked to take the office of Mayor. He knew of no compliment equal to it, and he knew of no individual who had filled the office of Mayor who had deserved so great a compliment as that which would be paid to Alderman Pickmere that day. (Hear, hoar.) He assured him if it was necessary, that the feeling which unanimously prevailed in the Council was that be

div.head: ST. HELEN'S COUNTY COURT.
div.p: ST. HELEN'S COUNTY COURT.

. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge. A HusßANn's LIABILITY.—Benjamin Williamson, grocer and provision dealer, sued Patrick Glynn, for £8 2s. ad., balance of an account for goeas stipplied.—Mr. Massey ap- peared for the plaintiff, and M. John Swift for defendant. There were two balances in the account, one for £5 6s. Bd. which was owing in May, and another of £2 15s. 6d. which had since been contracted.—Mr. Swift admitted that goods of the value of £2 15s. 6d. had been received since May, and not been paid for.—Plaintiff said defendant knew that. his wife traded with him on credit and had often stood at the door whilst she was inside the shop.—Mr. Swift said it was impossible to understand the books, but defendant's wife admitted that on May 16th, she owed about £2o.—ln de- fence he'submitted that defendant forbade his wife to pledge his credit, and had regularly given her 309. per week to keep his house. He could produce no documentary evidence, and the defendant's and plaintiff's books agreed to a certain extent. —He called the defendant, who said he did not know his wife bought goods on credit, and had expressly forbidden her to do so.—ln answer to his Honour, defendant said he did not know his wife was in debt until he received the County Court eammons.—Plaintiff was nonsuited.

BETTING EXTRAORDINARY.—Joseph Bradbury, having the I appearance of a workingman, sued 4ienry Marsh for £4 Ss. for a " business transaction."—Defeudant was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift,—Plaintiff said on the 20th September, he took four tickets in a "drawing" or lottery, organised by a man named Connelly. He paid is. each for two tickets, ss. for the third, and Ss. for the fourth. The last named ticket had an ensured prize of 10s, and its number corresponded to the name of a certaip horse which had to run in a race. Defendant laid a bet or £4 with the plaintiff that the ticket would not win a prize. The ticket did win a prize and de- fendant then refused to pay the money.—His Howur said it seemed to be a kinduf buabling.—Defeudant stated that the number on which he made the bet did not win a prize. —Plaintiff emphatically said it did.—liis Honour: I cannot help you. You must trust to his honour.—Philittlif was non-suited. 'PETTICOAT " GOVERNMENT. --- Willamn MCIC9I, black- smith, was sued by William Henry Wright, a wholesale tea dealer, for £5 Os. 3d.—Mr. Massey appeared or the defen- dant. Defendant's wife carried on a tea shop up to Septem- ber, 1875, when she deserted her husband. Defendant then had a large number of bills to pay which she had contracted, hly em proved by and borrowed some money with which to settl,eeatr denied the present claim. It was, however, e by the plaintiff's books that the amount claimed was owing, Honour made an order for ss. per week.

pursued. The establishment of a he, library in the town would certainly prove a blessing to, many in body and mind. tHnewaarlsdos assisting tthnastnalitio 4 ThemaennyP.eo.4lew speaker give a few books then read the had been the undersigned rate- payers f or:Yarded to Mr. Rimmer, which dwoacsu ma se n t followsw hiwhich pavers and workingmr.ox 'el Widnes, humbly ask you to take the necessary step", feer 'providing Widnes with a tree public library. We I,:,ed mot direct your attentten to the many advantages a. tee liiyeary would be to us workingmen, espe- cially du //lg the winter months, for there is scarcely any recrea:aon provided in the town except by the publicans. We, know the rates are high enough already, but we do not think much has. been expended for the benefit of those who reside in the lower end of the town. Mr. Brock, at the Science and Art Class meeting, said the total cost would not exceed one penny in the Z. We believe it could be done for one halfpenny in the £. Any decent sized shop would do for the library, and there are lots to be had which could be got for say £5O per annum. The librarian's salary would probably be £5O per annum, and the maintenance £5O; books per annum £50—making a total of £2OO, which does not mean more than one half- Penny in the L. St. Helens, Warrington, and Garston have free libraries, and we hope Widnes, with its 25000 inhabit- ants—chiefly workingmen—will soon possess one. We know your association is formed for protecting the rate- payers interests, but we don't think anyone would object to this slight increase, considering the great blessing it would be to the working classes. We feel sure, if you will take the matter in hand, the thing will soon be an accomplished fact. We hope, therefore, you will ask the Local Board to summon the necessary meeting, for which kindness your petitioners will ever feel grateful." (Here follow about 50 signatures.) Dr. O'Keeffe concluded by saying that the signatures were those of very respectable ratepayers, and it behoved them to see that Widnes was not behind in the march of intellect. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The CHAIRMAN remarked that the Board would not be able to deal with the question that day, as the petition which Dr. O'Keeffe had read was addressed to the Chairman of the Property Owners' and Ratepayers' Association. The Act expressly provided that the petition in favour of a meeting being called should be addressed to him (the Chairman.) The section read as follows: ' The Board of any district, being a place within the limits of any Improvement Act, shall, upon the requisition in writing of at least ten persons assessed to and paying the improvement rate, appoint a time not less than ten days, nor more than twenty days from the time of receiving such requisition, for a public meeting of the persons assessed to and paying such rate in order to determine whether the Act shall be adopted fer such district, and ten days' notice at least of the time, place, and object of such meeting shall be given by affixing the same on or near the door of every church or chapel within the district, and also by advertising the same in one or more of the newspapers published or cir- culated within the district, seven days at least before the day appointed for the meeting. If at such meeting two- thirds of such persons then present shall determine that the Act ought to be adopted for the district, the same shall thenceforth take effect and come into operation in such dis- trict, and shall be carried into effect according to the laws for the time being in force relating to such Board, or the Board may ascertain the opinions of the ratepaysrs by means of voting papers." If the petition came up for considera- tion at the Board meeting, the members would have to de- cide what should be done with it, and if it came to him before the time of their gathering, he should have to call a public meeting, at which he must be satisfied that the per- sons voting were ratepayers. The ascertaining of that would take a very long time if the meeting proved to be a very large one, and it would be a difficult thing to do; but the matter might be carried out very easily in such a town- ship as Widnes by the issuing of voting papers. If there was any opposition, the promoters of the Act could demand a poll. Dr. O'KEFFFE regretted that such an informality should have occurred. Personally, he felt sure,that every member of the Board would be glad to see a public library in Widnes, ia order that the intellectual, spiritual, and corporeal parts of the inhabitants at large might be benefited. (Laughter, and hear, hear). The CHAIRMAN believed that the Board would be quite ready to respond to an appeal upon the subject. This concluded the business.

div.head: _ LOCA.L BOARD,
div.p: _ LOCA.L BOARD,

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon. Major Cross occupied the chair, and there were also pre- sent lkiessrs. Heyes, Vey, Pankhurst, Gaskell, Handley/ o,Km.ffe, grachha,g, Shuttleworth, Sadler, Allen (clerk)' Roberts (engineer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). PRIVATE IMPROVEMENT EXPENSES. The CRAIRMAN read the following letter on this subject : —" Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., 21d, Nov., 1881.—Sir,-1 am directed by the Local Government Board' to advert to your letter of the 13th September, and to Info-An 1 the Widnes Local Board that the Board will instruct orA of their inspectors to visit the locality for the purpose cif inves- tigating the matter of the appeal of the Newton, Haydock, and Golbome Permanent Benefit Building Society against 1 the demand of the Local Board for the payment of certain I private improvement expenses. Due notice of the date of the inspector's visit will be given to the Local Board.-1 am, sir, your Obedient servant, WALTER SENDALL, assistant secretary.—To J. T. Allen, Esq., clerk to the Local Board, Widnes:"

PROPOSED IMPORTANT LOANS- Major Coss read a communication from the Public Works Loan Board, Loudon, stating that the Commissioners desired to remind the Local Board that they would not be authorised to advance to them after the 31st March, 1882, any money (either in respect of loans already granted or hereafter to be granted) unless notice of the sum required between the 31st March, 1882, and Ist April, 1883, be given to the Public Works Loan Board before the 31st December next. Ile next said that the following letter had since been received :—" Public Works Loan Board, 3, Bank Buildings, London, Nov., 1881.—Sir,-1 am directed to inform you that the PulalicWorks Loan Commissioners having had the application of the Widnes Local Beard for a loan of £20,000 under consideration, have resolved that such loan be granted for the purposes mentioned in the application, upon the security of a mortgage of the rates authorised under the Public health Act, 1875, for repayment of the principal by 60 equal half-yearly instalments, with interest at 31 per cent. per annum, on the principal sum from time to time re- maining unpaid; subject, however, to this Board's solicitor (with whom you are requested to communicate at the above address) being satisfied that the requirements of this Board and of the Acts of Parliament applicable to this case have been sufficiently complied with.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, E R. SPEARMAN, secretary..,— J. T. Allen,Esq., clerk to the Local Board, Widnes." THE LEVEL CROSSING NUISANCE. It was stated by the Chairman that the only further com- munication received as to the level crossings from the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company was a telegram sent that day from the secretary promising to write at once

on the TRB GOVERNMENT ArDITOR AND TRE BOARD. The following letter was read :—"240, Great Clowes- street, Higher Broughton, Manchester, 18th October, 1831. To the Local Board for the district of Widnes.—Gentlemen, —I beg to report that I have completed the audit of your accounts for the year ended Lady Day, 1381, and following the course which I considered it necessary to adopt at the audit for the year ended Lady Day, 1680, I have disallowed certain payments, the particulars of which you will find in your General, Gas, aad Water Ledgers. Having received from the Local Government Board a copy of a memorial from certain of your ratepayers, and an explanation by your chairman, with reference thereto, I thought it desirable not to close the audit until I had before me the result of the investigations which were promised by your Highway Com- mittee, the effect of which has been to shew that, during the past three years, a sum of £2,880 7s. 4d. has been spent on certain of your public roads, in excess of shat appears by the books, to have been expended on those streets. I have explained to the Local Government Board that your private improvement expenditure, for which no borrowing powers have been obtained, has really been made out of ad- vances by your treasurer, practically on security of the balances, due from private owners, but that, by the system of bookkeeping, hitherto adopted, it might appear that the same had been spent out of the unexpected balance of your loan for public street improvements. Had the loan accoum, for this purpose, .been keep separate, this unexpended balance would appear to be in hand, while your treasurer's general account would appear, by so much more, overdrawn, that it is already. I understand it is your intention to get in the balances due from private owners, and so repay the advances made by the treasurer, and, as I was assured, that the necessary alterations would be made in your books, with reference to the amount of £2,880 7s. 4d., above referred to, I did not alter them, but I have informed the Local Govern- ment that it is intended to credit the expenditure of General District Rate Account, and to debit the expenditure of Loan Account with this amount, and I trust this will be duly carried into effect. Your clerk, Mr. Allen, appears to understand clearly the requirements of the order for accounts, and particularly the necessity for keeping the Loan Accounts for district purposes, and under their respective sanctions, separate and distinct. This is a matter which I consider of great importance, and I trust you will support him, in adopting a principle, and carrying out a system, which you will, I think, agree with me, is not only perfectly sound, but most essential to good Local Government. I am, gentlemen, your obedient servant HENRY C. DARLINGTON, district auditor!' GAS AND WATER. The minutes of this committee, which were approved on the motion of Mr. GASICELL, seconded by Mr. HETES, stated that the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee as to reducing the staff expenses had been considered, and the committee could not see their way to make any reduction in the expenditure, The water in stock on the 19th ult. was 10,720,562 gals. A letter had been received from the Wid- nes Alkali Co., as to a reduction in the price of gas, but the committee had instructed Mr. Allen to reply that the com- mittee could not see their way to recommend a reduction at

present. HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.—IIILTON CHAPEL IMPROVEMENTS. The minutes of the Highway Committee were approved. The CHAIRMAN said the members would recollect that an agreement was come to some time ago between the trnstees of Milton Congregational chapel and the Board, by which the trustees agreed to convey to them a piece of land front- ing the road, on condition that the authority paid them £2OO, to be spent in building a wall in connection with the place of worship. As the work was proceeded with the surveyor would give a certificate as to the part which had been completed, and the proportion of money expended would be paid over. After a brief discussion as to the privileges granted by the trust deed of the chapel, which it appeared gave the trustees all the powers necessary to the carrying out of such an agreement, and a statement that the Board had agreed to do the flagging in connection with the place within a -fixed time, it was resolved on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. HAI•IDLEY, that the agreement should be signed. It was explained that the cost of the flagging could be included in next year's estimates. THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The Health Committee's minutes contained the report of the Medical Officer, which showed that the births during the month bad numbered 103, or 48.1 per 1,000; and the deaths 26, or 12.5 per 1,000. The deaths included those of eight children under oze year; four of children between one and five years. Four deaths had occurred from zymotic disease, and three inquests bad been held. This committee also re- ported that they could not see their way to any advantageous reduction of the staff. The market receipts for October had been 1,45 Os. 7d. being a decrease of Ll 15s. 2d., on the corresponding. month of last year. The fair ground receipts were £5 Is. 11d, more than for the corresponding fair last year. Mr. CAREY, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, re- ferred to the low death rate. He saw from the quarterly report of the Registrar General that the annual death rate during the three months ending September, in England and Wales, did not exceed 167 per 1,000 of the estimated popu- lation, and was no less than 29 below the average rate in the ten preceding quarters. The death rate in Widnes for the the same three months was 15.8 per 1,000, so that it was slightly under the average for England and Wales. THE HOSPITAL. The accounts presented for payment by the committee of the hospital amounted to £l6l 7s. 4d. The Surveyor re- ported that the westerly boundary wall had been blown down by the gale on the 14th ult., and that he had, owing Ca the building being unprotected, given instructions to Mr. T. Sadler to re-build the wall at once. Mr. HANDLE? proposed the passing of the minutes, and explained that the accounts included an item of £137 4s. 10d. for street making, over which the committee had no

power. Mr. CAREY seconded the motion, which was agreed to. ant. BEASLEY AND YEE BOOKS OF THE BOARD. Mr. HETES moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Committee, which stated that the Clerk had been instructed to wait upon the Local Government Board as to raising a large loan to pay off the smaller ones now in exis- tence. A list of the improvement accounts had been laid before the committee and instructions given to press for immediate payment ot several of them. The collections as shown by the collecting and deposit book for October amounted to £9,914 12s. Id. It was resolved that the Trea- surer's accounts be debited as follows :—Gas fund, £2,181 4s. 7d.; water fund, £2,888 3s. 5d.; general fund, £4.783 is.; West Bank sewerage fund, £lO2 3s. ld. Mr. Heyes said the committee had endeavoured to get the books and papers belonging to the Local Board from Mr. Beasley, but they could not do so, and it was exceedingly inconvenient for the Clerk to have to run over to that gentleman's off ce about every matter which needed enquiry. The CneaultAN : There is a letter here from him about g Ating the papers over to-morrow. (Laughter.) Mr. HEYES : If be will do so, so and good; Imt we have had so many promises from him. (Ironical laugh Mr. GASEELL seconded the motion for the adop:,on of the minutes, and it was passed. It was also resolved that the contract with Mr. Mather I for doing the work at the Bridge, Farnworth, be sealed. I THE PROPOSED FREE LIBRARY. Dr. O'KEEFFE said be bad received a letter from Mr. Jas. Itimmer, secretary of the Widnes Property Owners and Ratepayers Association. div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. TREF r BY THE WIFE OF AN ACTOR.—Elizabeth Conte, the wife of an actor and comic singer connected with the Diorama of the World, was charged with stealing, between the 10th and 24th October, two blankets and a night dress, from the house of Mrs. Harvey, in Lacey-street, Widnes. It appeared that while the troupe was in Widnes the prisoner lodged at Mrs. Harvey's, Lacey-street. While she was there nothing of a suspicious natune seems to have occurred; but after she left two blankets ant a nightdress were missed. Suspicion then attached to her, and information was given to the police. After same little time the missing articles were found at the shop of Mr. Jamieson, pawnbroker, in Anne-street West, where they had been pledged by a person answering to the description of the prisoner.—Selina Alberti Deakin, domestic servant, living with Mrs. Harvey, of Lacey-street, Widnes, said the prisoner lodged at the house from the 10th to the 24th October. After she left she missed two blankets, the property of her mistress, and the night- dress her own property. The blankets were kept in a box in the back bedroom. The prisoner had access to this room, but did not occupy it. When she discovered that the things had been stolen, her suspicion, from several causes, fell on the prisoner, and she gave information to the police of what had occurred.—P.C. Pitt said he went to Southport and found the prisoner there at a lodging-house. When charged with stealing the things, she admitted that she was guilty of the act.—The prisoner now pleaded in extenuation that she took the things because she was in want.—A young woman, con- nected with the diorama ref rred to, appeared in court, and said that while the prisoner was in Widnes her husband was earning £1 a week, and that she could not therefore have been in want.— By the Bench: She had been sent there that morning to state this, and had had her expenses paid.— The Bench, after a short deliberation, sent the prisoner to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Bibby (chairman), and Mr. F. H. Gossage. CAUTION TO FIREWORK SELLERS—CharIes Powell, shop- ' keeper, Waterloo-road, was summoned for selling fireworks to a lad under 13 years of age —Mr. Yearsley defended.— The case was proved by P.C. Ross and another coustable.— The Bench said that people who took out licenses to sell fireworks, ought in all cases to have responsible persons to sell them. Defendant would be fined 2s. fid. and costs.— Superintendent Barker remarked that he might, if he had chesen, have summoned the defendant for exposing the fire- works loosely in the window instead of having them in a glass case. SEntors CHARGE AGAINST A LICENSED VICTUALLER.— John Barran, of the Wat?rloo vaults, was summoned for per- drunkenness and selling been to a drunken man named Thomas Welsh.—Mr. Bartlett, Liverpool, appeared for defendant —The Inspector of Police and P.C. Liing were called to prove the case, and from their statement it appeared that on Sunday evening, the 23rd ultimo, the officers visited a beerhouse in Marsh-street, and found there the man Welsh and another. Welsh was drunk' and his companion was not sober, but they had no beer before them. They spoke to the landlord, who said that the men had not been sup- plied with anything and turned them out of the house. Shortly after they saw them go into the defendant's beer- house. Immediately after they visited the defendant's, and found each of the men with a pint of beer before him. The llnspector asked who had supplied the men with beer, and one of the barmen pointed out Welsh as the one to whom he bad served three pints of beer. Welsh then took hold of his pint and drunk of it, and whilst the Inspector was talk- ing to the barman; he finished it. The barman remarked "I saw that he was in drink," and then a second barman walked up and said "That is not his pint," but Welsh held it, and he only got it from him by main force. The officer asked Welsh his name, but he refused to give it. The Inspector said to the barman, "You must do your own duty, and get the man out of the house." The barman asked Welsh to go out, but he refused,though physical force was applied to him, on which the policeman locked him up, and he was brought before the Bench and fined 7s. dd. and costs.—Mr. Bartlett, for the defence, said he might, if he thought it desirable, deal with the conduct of the police in this case, and argue the question of whether it was better for the protectors of the public to try to prevent offences taking place, or catch the offenders after the law had been broken, but he would not go into this point. Welsh and his companion entered the vaults when the barmen were very busy. One of the two asked a barntan for three pints of beer. The barman, on seeing that one of them was drunk, refused to supply them. A man named Stanton, speaking of himself and a companion, said We are sober ; supply us with two pints of beer," which he did, but nothing was supplied to Welsh. Welsh, who was only in the place about three minutes, seized Stanton's pint, and put it to his lips, on which the barman took hold of him and forcibly ejected him. Several witnesses were called for the defence.—The Chairman remarked that from the way in which the wit- nesses had given their evidence, the magistrates believed the story of the police. At the same time, seeing the con- flicting nature of the evidence, they thought the ends of justice would he served by dismissing the case, on defendant paying costs, with a caution. STEALING COAL.—A woman named Ellen O'Grady was fined 20s. for stealing coal from the premises of Messrs. Pilkington, on the previous Wednesday. JUVENILE TIIEFT.—Thomw, John Mannion was sentenced to receive four strokes with the birch rod for having stolen half a crown, the money of Robert McMasters, of Whiston.

THE LiaecAsurita Cola. TRADE.—An adjourned meeting of the members of the Federation of Lancashire Miners was held at Wigan on Saturday afternoon. There were slaty-nine delegates present, representing nearly the whole of West Lancashire. It was reported that three delegates, who had I atended the conference during the week on the wages question had been dismissed by the masters, and a resolution was passed condemding tha action. Several delegates reported . that in some of the districts the employers had conceded an advance equal to the last redaction, and it was agreed that each pit set of.men be requested to report to the next meeting of the Federation, to be held in Manchester on the 29th in?t, the amouat of advance given at each colliery. It was aalird resolved to work only five days a week, and the president cretary were instructed to attend the funeral of thheiaetealVnlrd. Macdonald, as representing the miners of Lanus.r , that notice be sent to all employers asking for an advance for the day wagemen.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday. Dr. Steele presided; and there were also present Messrs. Norman, McDougall, Williams, Lake, Fisher, Whittaker, P. Speak- man, Hazlehurst, Timmins, Shaw, Handley, Briscoe, Meadowcroft, Linaker (law cleric), Brookes (secretary), Barker surveyor), and Monritz (medical officer).

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT: THE WATER AT THE FOUNTAIN. The report of Dr. Mouritz, medical officer, showed that the deaths registered in Runcorn during October numbered 15. One death had occurred at Halton-with-Runcorn, making the total number of deaths 16, representing a death rate of 12.9 per thousand per annum. Seven of them were due to diseages of the nervous system, two to pulmonary affections, two to marasmus. Abdominal disease, premature birth, measles, natural decay and exhaustion accounted for one each. Of the above deaths eight were those of children under four years and seven below one year. In conclusion, the Medical Officer said he had already reported the reason why he considered it necessary that the surveyor should cut off the water supplying the fountain opposite the Town Hall. The water contained a large proportion of alkaloids and other matter, rendering it totally unfit for drinking or

domestic purposes. A special report on the subject was laid upon the table, but not read, and was referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee for consideration. On: the proposition of Mr. NORMAN seconded by Mr. PHILIP SPEAKMAN, it was resolved that a printed notice should be placed upon the fountain, stating that the water was not fit for domestic use. Immediately before the termination of the meeting, the CHAIRMAN said that a letter had been received from J. Carter Bell, which stated that impurity in the fountain water was due to mineral and not to organic matter, and the liquid was not dangerous. OPPOSITION TO THE NEW BUILDING BYE-LAWS.

THE ANNUAL MEETING.

The SECIZETARY pointed out the inconvenience which arose from the annual meeting being held the day after the election of Mayors, and suggested that in future it should be held on the last Thursday in November or the first in De- sernber.

It was resolved that it should be held on the first Thurs- day in December. Mr. FAIR moved that the annual meeting should be held alternately at Manchester, Liverpool, and Preston. Several members spoke of the central position of Warring- ton, the large number of members residing within its vicinity, and its general convenienc,,. An amendment was made by Mr. HatsaLL that the meeting be held as heretofore at Warrington; and, after con- siderable discussion, Mr. FAIR withdrew his motion. The meeting will therefore be held at Warrington as usual. The meeting was adjourned to the second Thursday in December. The hostess of the Lion Hotel had provided an excellent dinner, to which full justice was done.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. EARLESTOWN WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CITURCII.—We have to congratulate the above for an exceedingly refined and elevating entertainment last Tuesday, which was characterised by a degree of excellence, versatility, and power that it is impossible to praise too highly. The artiste engaged was Mr. Powell Thomas (London), the renowned Cambrian virtuoso, and one of the brightest and most essen- tially intellectual entertainers of the day; who displayed brilliant varied gifts and graceful fertility in music and elocution. Nothing could possibly be better than this choice and—well-arranged programme. The recitals were vivid, life-like, and finely coloured embodiments. The lecturer's voice being exceedingly sympathetic and powerful, and dis• playing poetic enthusiasm, he catches the author's meaning, and interprets it by voice and gesture in the most intelligent and agreeable way. "The Bells " was conveyed (perfectly imitating a whole belfry of sounds) with so wonderful an approach to reality, that a thrill ran thr.ongli the spellbound audience,—it was marvellous, and roused the house to genuine enthusiasm. Great proficiency was also shown on several musical instruments, the songs and national fantasias being greatly enjoyed aud loudly applauded. This first- clais entertainment was so successful that .we may safely predict an overflowing assembly should Mr. Powell Thomas come again. Rev. James Allltt presided over a very large atrl respectatle audience. •

If they had animals which were equal to anything in England, it seemed to him there was no necessity to put a duty on their show, because it was really doing away with free trade, and putting on a duty to prevent the exhibition of stock from all parts of England. Mr. FITCRETT observed that their district was quite large enough to get a good show. Mr. FAIR said very few shows had such a wide district, and no show exhibited better stock.
